comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Not started. This tests whether one short SFT pass over the 10.05 checkpoint's own samples, with each malformed reasoning span repaired, removes extra think segments without lowering pass rate. If it does, consumers get a patched 10.05 instead of a full SFT re-run, which took 126 hours on 1,024 TPU v4 chips.

## Description

`open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05` (revision `8c76b22`) sometimes writes more than one reasoning segment in one assistant message: a stray `<|end_think|>` after the first block, or back-to-back blocks (#10400). This happens in 0.6% of thinking messages on bixbench-pi and 3.2% on bfclparity-pi, and RL raises the rate to 9.1% (Smartie RL step 14). #10518, #10519 and #10520 stop new data and RL from teaching or rewarding the habit, but the 10.05 checkpoint keeps it.

A re-run of the 10.05 SFT would cost about 129k TPU v4 chip-hours. The W&B run `grug-67b-sft-20260929-special-token-lr-full-ab-4750-grouped` (project `marin_moe_sft`) took 125.9 h for 4,750 steps on 1,024 chips at 94.9 s/step, plus 5.2 h in two crashed starts.

The patch trains on the model's own samples. Off-policy rows change think behavior quickly: four updates at 1e-5 on GLM-written rows cut closed think blocks from 255 of 284 to 53 of 387 ([curriculum SFT README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/77a3f6e1978a5bc331df0223079228418a10c9ff/experiments/post_training/curriculum_sft/README.md#L89-L101)). Training on clean samples alone gives a weak signal when only about 2% of samples are malformed. A repaired sample differs from the model's own output only at the malformed span, so its loss targets that decision.

## Hypothesis or Goal

One pass over at most 2,000 rows of repaired and clean samples, at a learning rate of at most 1e-5, cuts the held-out violation rate at least 10x and keeps held-out pass rate within 2 points of 10.05.

## Design

1. Baseline from stored samples (CPU only). #10000 sampled 10.05 8 times per SWE and terminal pivot prompt, with thinking on, temperature 1.0, special tokens kept and no reasoning parser ([runs.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/33f37f1c9a36368102d3c2d4c5d13beddb8a2263/experiments/post_training/pivotrl/runs.py#L128-L139)). The raw messages are in `message_json` under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/dml/pivotrl/<candidates>/pass-rates/grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-262k-20261005/2026.10.09/`. Classify each sample as well-formed (one `<|start_think|>` at the start and one `<|end_think|>`), stray end, back-to-back, or orphan close, and count `finish_reason=length` separately. If fewer than 0.5% of samples are malformed, switch to tool-use chat prompts like bfclparity-pi.
2. Rows (CPU only), from training candidates only. A repaired row takes a malformed sample that did not hit the token limit. Its reasoning is everything before the last `<|end_think|>`, with inner think tokens replaced by a blank line. Its reply and tool calls are unchanged. A clean row is a well-formed sample from the same prompts, unchanged. Use equal numbers of repaired and clean rows, keep samples whatever their task score, and put the loss on the final assistant turn only.
3. Train three arms from 10.05, one pass each, with an export at mid-pass and one at the end:

   | Arm | Rows | Learning rate |
   |---|---|---|
   | T-low | repaired + clean | 1e-6 |
   | T-high | repaired + clean | 1e-5 |
   | C-high | clean only, same row count | 1e-5 |

   Two trainers fit. The arm trainer in #10327 (prebuilt `input_ids` and `loss_weights`, batch 16 × 32k, constant learning rate, 4×8 H100) needs a 10.05 entry in its [`PARENTS`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/01d104874e0c3c20fc38a65645b466d3c02bde8b/experiments/post_training/agentic_sweep/arms.py#L94-L107) table and rows in its manifest format. The PivotRL SFT path in #10000 already trains on the final turn of pivot prompts.
4. Measure on the held-out pivot rows, 4 samples per row, with the same settings for 10.05 and every arm (`heldout_baseline_step` and `heldout_eval_step` in #10000). The primary metric is the violation rate. The guards are pass rate, the share of samples that close their span, and the `finish_reason=length` rate. Sample enough rows for 10.05 to show at least 20 violations. Then run bfclparity-pi and bixbench-pi on the best arm and compare with the 10.05 runs from 2026-10-17.

Decision rule:
- Success: the violation rate falls at least 10x and its 95% interval excludes the 10.05 rate. Pass rate stays within 2 points, and the span-closing and length-stop rates do not get worse.
- If T-low succeeds, publish 10.05 with the patch as the base for consumers and add the patch to the post-training recipe.
- If T-high succeeds and C-high does not, the repair is what works. Adopt T-high if the guards hold.
- If C-high also succeeds, clean on-policy samples are enough and the repair step can go.
- If no arm succeeds, try a format reward in RL (#10520) before an SFT re-run.

If the patch works, repeat T-low on v0.1 (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14`, the base in #10213), which has extra segments in 9.1% of thinking messages.

Estimated cost: 100–150 H100-hours, about one day. Each arm takes 20–25 H100-hours, mostly model loading, compilation and export; its 65M padded tokens train in minutes. Held-out sampling takes about 8 H100-hours per checkpoint, and bfclparity-pi plus bixbench-pi take 20–40 H100-hours for one arm.

## Status

Not started.

## Links

* Logbook: this issue
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:
* Parent: #10400. Trainers: #10327, #10000. Related: #10428 (format SFT on Hero).

## Decision Log

- 2026-10-22: Patch the existing 10.05 checkpoint before considering an SFT re-run, which costs about 129k TPU v4 chip-hours. Train on repaired on-policy rows, for the reasons in the description.

## Conclusion

# Proposed Fix

1. Audit the stored 10.05 SWE and terminal samples on CPU. Split by candidate row before selecting training examples; classify each assistant message by delimiter pattern and count `finish_reason=length` separately. Report counts by prompt family and sample ID. If violations are below 0.5%, sample tool-use prompts as the issue specifies. Size the held-out set to show at least 20 baseline violations.
2. Build a versioned manifest and at most 2,000 final-turn examples from training candidates only: equal repaired and unchanged clean rows, plus a clean-only comparator with the same row count. Exclude length stops, preserve reply text and tool calls, record source sample IDs and before/after delimiter counts, and test tokenized renderings for each malformed class and the loss mask.

Check the actual GPU-hour estimate before launch because this path currently allocates 8×8 H100 rather than the 4×8 arm trainer cited in the issue. Coordinate changes with #10000 instead of opening a parallel trainer PR.
4. Evaluate 10.05 and every export on the same held-out rows with four samples per row and identical serving settings. Report violation classes, pass rate, closed-span share, and length-stop rate with 95% intervals clustered by prompt. Apply the issue's 10× reduction and 2-point pass-rate guards before running bfclparity-pi and bixbench-pi on the selected arm. ## Goal

Run a weight-merging loop on spare Marin compute: merge Snowball checkpoints on CPU (reserved v4 hosts in us-central2-b), screen the merges cheaply with TPU vLLM on preemptible single-host slices, and promote winners to the H100 policy evaluation. This issue tracks the project end to end.

- vLLM fork `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`, tpu-inference `ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d` (head of marin-community/tpu-inference#27, stacked on #29 and #28), applied job-locally

- S = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02` @ `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`

## Status

| Step | State |
|---|---|
| Inventory, feasibility, campaign matrix | done 2026-10-15 |
| Parents S, C, A5, M staged and sha256-verified in `gs://marin-us-central2/scratch/karan/rsi-merge/parents/` | done 2026-10-16 |
| Merge toolkit: allowlisted BF16 to F32 widening for M's router biases (branch `task/197`) | done, no PR yet |
| TPU scoring smoke test | done: TPU scores 6-7 points below H100 |

| Quantized serving on v5e | blocked: the pinned fork rejects every quant config for GrugMoE |
| Localize the TPU gap | in progress (#10250) |
| Iteration-one merges (3 recipes) | not started, waiting on the scoring path |

## MATH500 scores for S, same model revision, same Evalchemy pin, same effective sampling

| Server | Score |
|---|---|
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-03 record | 0.950 |
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-17 | 0.944 |
| TPU v6e-8 TP8 bf16 (two runs) | 0.878, 0.882 |
| TPU v5p-8 TP4 bf16 | 0.884 |

Per item: 421 right everywhere, 39 right on both H100 runs and wrong on TPU, 12 wrong everywhere. The 39 are long solutions; 22 of them drift onto a different problem mid-solution.

## The TPU gap (#10250)

Teacher-forced logprobs on the same 10 items match the H100 within noise up to token 2047 and diverge from exactly token 2048, which is S's `sliding_window` (`global_every` 4). The gap grows to about 0.14 nat mean absolute logprob difference by 3-4k tokens.

Ruled out: truncation, thinking mode, sampling (Evalchemy strips temperature and seed, both servers run vLLM defaults), batch dependence, sharding degree and chip generation (v5p-8 TP4 scores the same), cross-request contamination, mask off-by-one (training, FA3 and the TPU kernel all keep the last W tokens including self), KV block eviction (the TPU runner keeps one full-attention cache group), per-layer window plumbing (reaches the TPU kernel unchanged; global layers get no window), KV cache dtype (bf16 on both).

Not valid controls at this pin: `grugmoe_attention_mode=dense` (never read by the vLLM model), a GPU TP8 run (GPU GrugMoE requires TP=1), the experimental batched RPA kernel (fails to compile: its SMEM schedule is sized from a reported capacity above the compiler's 1 MiB limit).

A standalone probe of the pinned ragged-paged-attention v3 kernel against its dense reference with random inputs passes 22 cases around the window boundary (error flat at bf16 noise). Random inputs spread attention over about 2048 keys, so that probe cannot see an edge or sink effect. Running now: a kernel probe with peaky scores, a BOS-like sink key and position-bucket values, and a TPU serving control with the window disabled.

Consequence for the loop: TPU vLLM cannot rank merges until this is fixed. One H100x8 MATH500 run costs about 14 minutes of box time per candidate.

## Related

- #10250 TPU sliding-window divergence
- #9400 tpu-inference pin bump and hardware checks
- #8323 Snowball TPU serving
- #7555 earlier long-context divergence on TPU
- marin-community/tpu-inference#28 custom router selections, #29 host storage release, #27 TP8 head padding (the stack every TPU run here used)
- Two Evalchemy integration gotchas found on the way: the pinned Evalchemy strips `temperature` and `seed` from requests, so the server's defaults apply; and marin's FineStore result reader expects native results JSON while Evalchemy `3bb8278` writes parquet tables, so the parent eval job reports FAILED although the child succeeded and the score is in `data/evalchemy_results/`.

## Open decisions

1. Score iteration-one merges on H100 now, or wait for the TPU fix.
2. Open a PR for the merge-toolkit change on `task/197`.
3. File the Iris autoscaler tier-blocking issue (a v6e-4 group in backoff blocks v6e-8 demand in the same zone).

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
## TPU serving defect localized: global attention layers get the sliding window

Follow-up to the seven-way comparison above. The TPU-side defect is now named and fixed by a config override; the proper fix is in tpu-inference.

**What happens.** tpu-inference registers a vLLM general plugin (`tpu_inference/layers/vllm/__init__.py`, `register_layers` -> `_register_grugmoe`). Whenever the TPU stack is present it sets `_CONFIG_REGISTRY["grug_moe"] = GrugMoeHfConfig`, replacing the vLLM fork's `GrugMoeConfig`. `GrugMoeHfConfig` (`tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py`) is a plain `PretrainedConfig` with name aliases; it never sets `layer_types`. The fork's `GrugMoeConfig` sets `layer_types` from `grug_moe_layer_types(num_layers, global_every)`. Plugins load in `EngineArgs.__post_init__`, before the model config is built, so on TPU `hf_text_config.layer_types` is `None`. vLLM then sets `cache_config.sliding_window = 2048` (arg_utils: "only set CacheConfig.sliding_window if the model is all sliding window"), and the fork's GrugMoE model, which passes `per_layer_sliding_window=None` for its 7 global layers (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25 of 26), gets 2048 for them through the `Attention.__init__` fallback. A static trace of the TPU engine shows all 26 layers at `sliding_window=2048`. On H100 the plugin is absent, the fork config is used, and the engine builds 4 KV cache groups with the global layers unwindowed. The fork model derives its own layer pattern from `global_every`, so nothing crashes; the window is just applied to the wrong layers.

**Verification.** Passing `--hf-overrides '{"layer_types": [...]}'` (the fork's list: `full_attention` at 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25, `sliding_attention` elsewhere) changes the trace to 7 layers at `None` and 19 at 2048, with 4 KV cache groups. Teacher-forced probe (same 10 MATH500 items, 35,801 positions) against the exact-window eager reference, mean |delta logprob|:

| positions | TPU, override | TPU, default | H100 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2048 | 0.015-0.018 | 0.015-0.018 | 0.014-0.016 |
| 2048-2304 | 0.013-0.016 | 0.023-0.038 | 0.012-0.014 |
| 2304-3072 | 0.015-0.017 | 0.054-0.080 | 0.014-0.016 |
| 3072+ | 0.012-0.015 | 0.132-0.142 | 0.011-0.014 |

TPU with the override vs H100 directly: 0.011-0.017 at every position. MATH500 with the override (Evalchemy 3bb8278, seed 19311, same settings as the TPU runs above): **0.940** (470/500, 500 generated and scored, 1421 s), against 0.878-0.884 for TPU without it and 0.944 / 0.950 for the two H100 runs. The gap is closed.

**Fix.** Proper fix is in tpu-inference: `GrugMoeHfConfig` should set `layer_types` the same way the fork does, or the plugin should not replace a registry entry the fork already provides. tpu-inference `main` at 340444337772 (2026-10-19) still has the overwrite. Until then, TPU serving of any GrugMoE checkpoint whose `config.json` lacks `layer_types` needs the override above. Pins: vLLM fork fb02daf, tpu-inference ae387b8, Step12 @50fe2f488aee.

| vLLM TP16, same slice and model | warmed, fixed 128-token outputs, concurrency 8 | 675.5 tok/s |

At concurrency 4, the engine mostly ran batches of 1-2 sequences. So the 4-slot gain is smaller than the slot count suggests.

Model load: about 480-530 s for Levanter, against 1,077 s to readiness for vLLM, which includes about 450 s of compile.

**Estimated full MATH500 time**

The H100 reference run generated 985,550 tokens on the same 500 items.

| Rate | Estimated generation time |
|---|---:|
| 12.1 tok/s | 22.7 h |
| 13.8 tok/s | 19.8 h |
| 19.1 tok/s | 14.3 h |
| vLLM v4-32, measured | 33 min (1,991 s) |

On this hardware, Levanter is about 26-36x slower than vLLM. Earlier work in #3826 measured 762 vs 7,940 tok/s, about 10x, on a different model and setup.

**Configuration for the full run**

- 2 sequence slots at ctx 16384 (260 KV pages). 4 slots at 16384 ran out of memory at 31.46 GiB per chip. 4 slots at 8192 fits, but 27 of the 500 H100 responses exceed 8,192 tokens.
- We have not yet measured the throughput of the 2-slot, 16384 setting on a full workload. The table above brackets it.
- A batching bug in the native JAX ragged paged attention kernel was fixed job-locally: it hit a DMA semaphore error (E0200) when the last row of a 2-sequence batch had zero queries. The fix aligns the metadata to the rows that have queries.
- Teacher-forced logprobs from batched and serial runs agree within noise: mean |dlogp| 0.013-0.014 and top-1 disagreement of 0.6-0.7%. Item 303 matches the exact-window oracle at the same level as H100 and vLLM.

The final MATH500 score will follow when the run completes.

issues.title: Weight-merging RSI loop on spare TPU compute: tracking issue

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Not started. This reruns the Grug single-turn long-SWE PivotRL recipe from the 10.05 SFT with #10542 applied, so rollouts with malformed reasoning spans get reward 0, and asks whether that alone stops the AIME24 decline and the entropy collapse that the 2026-10-14 run showed.

## Description

PivotRL on `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05` (revision `8c76b22`) has not produced a usable checkpoint. The 2026-10-14 single-turn long-SWE run ([W&B `lxm4qlxv`](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/pivot-rl/runs/lxm4qlxv): GRPO, lr 4e-6, KL 0.01, 64 prompts x 8 samples, 2,048 generated tokens) raised held-out pivot accuracy from 0.285 to 0.390 by step 10, while AIME24 fell from 0.830 to 0.803 by step 2 and to 0.76-0.77 by step 10, pass@8 on the pivots fell from 0.89 to 0.70, and policy entropy fell from 0.448 to 0.157. Longer pivot-only runs on the same SFT did worse: forty Terminal updates cost 36 points on AIME24, and ninety SWE updates left 1 of 248 SWE-bench Verified trials solved (#10214, "Why 20%"). The same recipe on `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507` held AIME24 at 0.917 and raised SWE-bench Verified from 4.6% to 15.6% in 10 steps (#10546), so the recipe works on a model that does not emit malformed spans.

The 10.05 checkpoint writes stray `<|end_think|>` markers, second reasoning spans and unclosed spans (#10400), and RL amplified them: in #10214 arm A the malformed rate rose from 2.8% at step 1 to 10.2% at step 12, and 6 to 118 malformed rollouts per step were rewarded (#10520 baseline). Before #10542, `final_answer_text` graded the text after the last end marker, so a malformed turn could score and its tool calls ran. #10542 grades any rollout with a malformed turn as a submission failure with reward 0. An 8-step rerun of arm A with the fix rewarded no malformed rollout and cut the malformed rate to 1.4-1.6% in steps 4-7, against 4.6-7.1% in the baseline ([result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10520#issuecomment-6368038579)). That rerun measured the violation rate and RLVR validation reward only. It did not run AIME24 or SWE-bench, and it had no pivots.

The SFT-side repair of 10.05 (#10521) was closed as not planned on 2026-10-23, so the RL-side rejection is the only fix in place.

## Hypothesis or Goal

With malformed-span rollouts rejected, the Grug long-SWE PivotRL recipe keeps AIME24 within 0.02 of 0.830 through step 10 and policy entropy above 0.3. AIME24 is the canary: it fell first in the baseline, by step 2. If it still falls to 0.80 or below by step 5 while the malformed rate stays under 2%, the format violations were not the cause and the drift is a recipe problem (KL coefficient, learning rate, entropy bonus), which #10214 lists as the next fix. SWE-bench Verified is measured only if the canary passes.

## Design

One arm, one seed, 10 steps, matched to `lxm4qlxv` as its W&B config records it: the 10.05 SFT, the same selected SWE pivots (`users/dml/pivotrl/swe/skyrl-long-selected/6cf4f9d5…/train.parquet`), the `nemo` grader through `pivot_reward`, GRPO at lr 4e-6 with KL 0.01 to a frozen reference, entropy loss off, sequence-mean loss, 64 prompts x 8 samples, 2,048 generated tokens, eval every 5 steps. The runtime is main's vendored SkyRL with #10542, as in the arm A rerun, with that rerun's three launch fixes. The launcher adapts the arm A rerun file. Trajectory retention keeps every training rollout (`sample_fraction` 1), as lxm4qlxv did, so the malformed-span scan has the full population. HF exports at steps 2, 5 and 10.

Steps:

1. Two-step smoke on a few nodes with the real pivot rows. The arm A rerun never exercised `pivot_reward`, and its terminal pivots failed in session setup.
2. Train 10 steps. Stop if AIME24 at step 5 is at or below 0.80, the baseline's level.
3. Per step, from retained trajectories with the #10520 scan: malformed rate by form and the count of malformed rollouts with reward > 0, which must be 0. Held-out pivot accuracy from the in-run eval; entropy, KL and tokens per response from W&B.
4. AIME24 avg@10 at steps 2, 5 and 10 under the October 5 verified policy. Step 0 is 0.830 on the same policy and is reused.
5. SWE-bench Verified, 500 tasks, at step 10 only, and only if AIME24 held, paired against the 10.05 reference run (.260) in the same cohort.

Decision rules:

- AIME24 within 0.02 of 0.830 at step 10, no rewarded malformed rollout, entropy above 0.3: the fix stops the collapse. Run the step-10 SWE-bench eval. If it is up by more than two paired standard errors (about 4 points), apply the fix to #10214 arm B and run past 8 steps.
- AIME24 at or below 0.80 by step 5 with the malformed rate under 2%: the fix is not sufficient. Stop. The next experiment changes one recipe knob, KL coefficient or learning rate.
- AIME24 holds but the malformed rate passes 3% after step 8 through second spans, as the arm A rerun hinted at step 8: report it and add the #10519 checks before any longer run.

Not in this plan: steps 11 and 12, SWE-bench at step 5, re-measuring step 0, a second seed, held-out evals outside the training loop. They return only if the canary passes.

## Status

Not started.

## Links

* Logbook: this issue
* W&B Report:
* Grug baseline run: https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/pivot-rl/runs/lxm4qlxv
* Format fix: #10520, #10542; its arm A rerun: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10520#issuecomment-6368038579
* Malformed spans in 10.05: #10400; closed SFT repair: #10521
* Qwen rerun of the same recipe: #10546
* Mixed-domain PivotRL and the pivot-only dose data: #10214
* Pivot selection and graders: #9933, #10000

## Decision Log

- 2026-10-23: Test the RL-side fix on the pivot-only recipe before touching the recipe's KL, learning rate or entropy bonus, so one change is tested at a time.
- 2026-10-23: Keep 10.05 as the base. 09.21 leaks extra reasoning segments more often (2.5% vs 0.6% of thinking messages on bixbench-pi, #10400), also drifted under RL (#9735), and has no pass rates, pivot selections or current-policy baselines. Switching bases would also break the matched comparison with lxm4qlxv.
- 2026-10-23: Cut the plan to one 10-step arm with an AIME24 stop rule at step 5 and a conditional SWE-bench eval at step 10.
- 2026-10-23: Scanned all six #10214 arms for malformed spans before launch ([results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10585#issuecomment-6372246722)). The rate rises in every arm, and the arm with the most malformed spans at step 12 is the arm that lost the most Math500 at both seeds. The lxm4qlxv trajectories are gone, so the pivot run itself could not be scanned. Corrected the recipe to the W&B config: 64 x 8 samples, 2,048 tokens.

## Conclusion

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Before launching, a CPU-only check can test the premise on runs that already exist. The #10520 baseline scan ran only on #10214 arm A. The same scan on the retained trajectories of arms B and C, and of the Grug pivot run `lxm4qlxv` if it retained any, answers two questions for free:

- Did the malformed rate rise in the pivot run alongside its AIME24 drop? Arm A went from 2.8% at step 1 to 10.2% at step 12, and by step 12 more than half of the malformed rollouts were unclosed spans that ended the turn with no answer, which scores zero on every benchmark. If the pivot run shows the same shape, the premise of this issue is already half confirmed. If its rate stayed flat while AIME24 fell, the fix alone will not rescue it and the plan changes before launch.
- Did arms B and C differ from A in malformed rate? If they did, the B vs A and B vs C comparisons in #10214 carry a format confound that nobody has measured.

Running it now. Results follow in this thread.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Scan results for all six #10214 arms (both seeds, training phase, 64k to 75k retained rollouts per arm). The Grug pivot run `lxm4qlxv` could not be scanned: its run directory under `swe-behavior-pilot/runs` no longer exists on S3, only the Qwen pivot runs remain there. Arm A at seed 42 reproduces the #10520 baseline table to the rollout, so the scan is the same measurement.

| Arm | Step 1 | Step 4 | Step 8 | Step 12 | Peak | Rewarded malformed rollouts, steps 1-12 | Unclosed share of malformed, step 12 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A seed 42 | 2.9% | 7.1% | 3.5% | 10.2% | 10.2% (step 12) | 439 | 54% |
| B seed 42 | 2.3% | 1.2% | 3.1% | 7.9% | 7.9% (step 12) | 241 | 37% |
| C seed 42 | 2.2% | 1.7% | 0.8% | 6.2% | 6.2% (step 12) | 134 | 53% |
| A seed 43 | 2.7% | 2.3% | 6.9% | 4.7% | 7.7% (step 6) | 437 | 20% |
| B seed 43 | 2.2% | 2.3% | 2.6% | 6.5% | 6.8% (step 11) | 256 | 59% |
| C seed 43 | 2.2% | 1.7% | 4.1% | 4.9% | 6.5% (step 7) | 332 | 28% |

RLVR rows only, so the arms are compared on the same prompts (pivot rows are 20% of B and C):

| Step | A s42 | B s42 | C s42 | A s43 | B s43 | C s43 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 2.9% | 2.9% | 2.7% | 2.7% | 2.8% | 2.7% |
| 4 | 7.1% | 1.5% | 1.9% | 2.3% | 2.5% | 2.0% |
| 8 | 3.5% | 3.8% | 1.0% | 6.9% | 3.0% | 5.1% |
| 12 | 10.2% | 9.9% | 8.2% | 4.7% | 8.0% | 6.4% |

What this says:

- **The rise is universal.** Every arm starts at 2.2-2.9% and ends at 4.7-10.2%, with second spans and unclosed spans taking over from stray ends after step 8 in all six runs. It is a property of the recipe, not of arm A.
- **The arm that lost the most Math500 is the arm with the most malformed spans, at both seeds.** #10214 reports the largest step-12 Math500 loss for A at seed 42 and B at seed 43. Those are the two arms with the highest step-12 malformed rate here (10.2% and 6.5% against the other two arms at each seed) and the two highest unclosed shares (54% and 59%). An unclosed span that ends the turn has no answer and scores zero on every benchmark. Two seeds is a small sample, but the ordering matches on both.
- **The B vs A comparison at step 8 is not confounded in a consistent direction.** On RLVR rows at step 8, B is above A at seed 42 (3.8% vs 3.5%) and below A at seed 43 (3.0% vs 6.9%). The pooled B above A result on SWE-bench Verified stands.
- **Pivot rows are mostly clean.** SWE and Terminal pivots run at 0.6-2.0% malformed across all steps, under the 4,096-token cap. B at seed 43 still rewarded 95 malformed SWE pivots, because the `nemo` grader compares the tool call and does not see the stray think segment before it.
- **Rewarded malformed rollouts: 134 to 439 per arm over 12 steps.** None of these would have been rewarded under #10542.
- **Under RL the policy learns to always open a span.** In arm A the share of turns with no span falls from 14.5% at step 1 to 1.9% at step 12. The fixed rerun in #10520 showed the same move, from 2,090 no-span turns at step 4 to 296 at step 8, and then the growth shifted to second spans.

Implications for this experiment: the malformed rate is a usable early signal, and the scan is cheap enough to run after every few steps. The seed-43 arms show the rate can rise sharply mid-run (A to 7.7% at step 6) and fall again, so a single-step reading is noisy; use two consecutive steps as the stop rule does.

Method: every sampled turn is classified on its token IDs (`<|start_think|>` 128002, `<|end_think|>` 128003) with the #10542 rules; a turn that stopped on the length limit inside its span counts as truncation. A rollout is malformed when any turn is. Scanner: `experiments/post_training/reasoning_spans/scan_reasoning_spans.py`, to be committed with the launcher. Full per-step and per-source tables for all six arms are in the JSON output alongside it.

One correction to the Design above: the W&B config for `lxm4qlxv` shows 64 prompts x 8 samples, 2,048 generated tokens, GRPO, lr 4e-6, KL 0.01, entropy loss off, frozen reference, eval every 5 steps. The "16 samples, 8,192 tokens" came from the Qwen rerun (#10546). The Design is being corrected to the Grug numbers.

issues.body:
The [October 14 MarinSkyRL nightly](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/actions/runs/38578876774) stopped CatCount before Iris submission. `config/update-external.py MarinSkyRL` upgraded `marin-taskcompendium` to `0.2.175.dev38563438335` but retained `marin-rigging` at `0.2.149.dev37775727576`. Its installed-metadata check failed:

```text
The package `marin-taskcompendium` requires `marin-rigging==0.2.175.dev38563438335`, but `0.2.149.dev37775727576` is installed
```

OPD and Grug passed in the same run. The [October 13 nightly](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/actions/runs/38432357748) passed all three lanes.

Reproduce:
1. In a Marin main checkout, set the `marinskyrl` source in `config/external/MarinSkyRL/pyproject.toml` to `rev = "b1edaa10d59ce9717d4c87f7b7fede119eb011c2"`.
2. Run `uv run config/update-external.py MarinSkyRL`.

Expected: the refreshed lock installs a Rigging version compatible with the selected TaskCompendium release, passes `uv pip check`, and lets CatCount submit to Iris.

[The updater](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/config/update-external.py) upgrades only `marinskyrl`. The external project's Rigging override has a lower bound of `0.2.144.dev37540375919`, which permits the stale locked wheel to survive the refresh. [#9929](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9929) fixed an earlier Git-source mismatch; this failure occurs with published wheels.

comments.body: 🤖 Fixed by SkyRL vendoring (#10458), which removed the MarinSkyRL external lock; vendored SkyRL now takes Rigging from the same checkout, so the mismatch cannot recur.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Investigate having asynchronous "ops" agents which scan our Iris cluster(s) for various types of activity:

  * security anomalies - new users or jobs appearing, GCP resource or permission changes
  * performance anomalies - JAX jobs which are running slower than expected, data loading warnings
  * stability - check cluster health statistics, controller responsiveness, triage slowdowns
  * failures - activate in response to health alerts, triage, attempt to fix, escalate
  * cleanup - identify patterns in human/agent processes, codify them into runbooks or skills

Where should these live? Likely independent of our Iris controller to have a separate failure domain, perhaps as Github actions, or on a dedicated agent service like github.com/rjpower/weaver? They will require sensitive permissions, so alternatively a GCP VM & locked down agent controls would be valuable.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + actionability check
- [x] Survey existing ops/agent infra (skills, GitHub Actions, Iris health code)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PR/issue on SREbots)
- [x] Post analysis + proposed approach (design issue → no PR per agent scope rules)

This is a design/research issue (new cross-cutting infra, no concrete bug or definition of done), so per the agent workflow I'm posting analysis for a human to steer, not a PR.

# Research

We already have most of the building blocks for SREbots — they just aren't pointed at the live cluster yet. Two patterns exist today:

1. **Scheduled Claude agents via GitHub Actions cron** (`.github/workflows/ops-*.yaml`) that shell into `infra/scripts/nightshift_*.py` and spawn Claude Code. These run on `ubuntu-latest` with no cluster credentials — they only touch the repo (cleanup, doc-drift, CI-health).
2. **Failure-triggered triage agents** (`.github/actions/claude-triage`) fired by the canary ferries on failure — these already do collect → diagnose → file-issue → Slack.

What's missing is exactly what this issue asks for: a *proactive, periodic* agent with read access to cluster state. None exists; grep finds no "SREbot"/"ops agent" loop. ("weaver" in our ops logs is the external issue tracker, not an agent service.)

**Relevant code**
- [`.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-cleanup.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-nightshift-cleanup.yaml) + [`infra/scripts/nightshift_cleanup.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/scripts/nightshift_cleanup.py) - cron→Claude pattern to copy
- [`.github/actions/claude-triage`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/.github/actions/claude-triage) - collect→diagnose→file-issue→Slack, already built
- [`.agents/agents/ops-steward.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/agents/ops-steward.md) - read-only ops persona to base scan agents on
- [`lib/iris/OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/OPS.md) - diagnostic commands + SQL the agent would run
- [`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller) - `worker_health.py`, `audit_logging.py`, `pruner.py` (health/audit signals to scan)

Existing postmortems in [`.agents/ops/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/.agents/ops) are the concrete anomaly classes to detect (stuck `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` backlog, zombie/recycled-IP workers, scheduler-thread freezes, orphaned slices, taint timeouts).

# Proposed approach

The hosting question is the crux. Recommendation, in order:

**Where they run — split by failure domain and privilege:**
- **Phase 1 (low-risk, no new infra):** read-only scanners as GitHub Actions cron, same shape as nightshift. Auth to the cluster via the controller's RPC endpoint using a **read-only/observer credential**, not GCP admin. Out-of-band from the Iris controller → separate failure domain, which is the stated requirement. Output = ops-log file + `/file-issue` + Slack on high severity. Strictly no mutations.
- **Phase 2 (privileged actions):** anything needing GCP resource/permission visibility or remediation moves to a **dedicated locked-down GCP VM** with a narrowly-scoped service account and an allowlist of commands — not GitHub-hosted runners, which shouldn't hold standing cluster-admin secrets. This is where a `rjpower/weaver`-style hosted agent would slot in if we want a persistent service rather than cron.

**The five categories map to different triggers, so don't build one mega-bot:**
- security / GCP-permission drift → privileged (Phase 2), read GCP audit logs
- performance (slow JAX, data-loading warnings) → cron scan of finelog/W&B (Phase 1)
- stability (controller responsiveness, health stats) → cron scan of controller RPC (Phase 1)
- failures → **reuse the existing `claude-triage` action**, just add health-alert triggers alongside canary-failure triggers
- cleanup → already partly covered by nightshift; extend to codify recurring `.agents/ops/` patterns into runbooks/skills

**Suggested first slice (smallest useful, fully Phase-1):** `ops-sre-scan.yaml` (cron, e.g. every 4h) → `infra/scripts/sre_scan.py` → Claude with the `ops-steward` persona running the read-only diagnostics in `OPS.md`, emitting a finding only when a threshold trips (stuck-QR count, dead-worker count, reconcile latency). File an issue / Slack ping per finding; never mutate. This validates the credential boundary and output plumbing before we grant any write/GCP scope.

Open questions for a human before implementation:
1. Is a read-only controller/observer credential available, or does scanning require minting one?
2. Phase-2 host preference: dedicated GCP VM vs. an external agent service (weaver)?
3. Should failures route through the existing `claude-triage` action, or a separate SRE path?

Happy to turn the Phase-1 slice into a concrete PR (workflow + script + skill) once the credential and hosting questions are settled.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Three matched mixed-domain RLVR runs from the Grug Datakit SFT (October 5) test whether a share of [PivotRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) pivots improves SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite without hurting the other domains, and whether pivot selection matters: RLVR alone, RLVR with selected SWE and Terminal pivots at 20% of prompts, and RLVR with random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share. Two optional arms move the selected share to 10% and 30%. Every arm stops at 12 steps. Status: all three arms trained 12 steps at seed 42 and were evaluated at steps 4, 8 and 12; [results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6305992938). B is the only arm above the SFT on SWE-bench Verified (+8.8 points at steps 4 and 8, p=.0001; +4.8 at step 12), C never transfers, and every arm drifts on Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12. A seed-43 replicate finished 45 of 48 evaluations ([final](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6357439611)). At step 8, B beats C at both seeds (+10.0 and +12.6) and beats A at both seeds (+9.2 and +3.0; pooled +6.1, p<.0001), with no loss on the reasoning benchmarks. By step 12 the arms no longer separate and every arm loses Math500 and MMLU-Pro. B at step 8 is the checkpoint to report, and running longer needs a drift fix.

## Hypothesis

Pivots that the SFT policy's own pass rates select (#9933), rewarded by #9933's deterministic verifiers, improve SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite at 20% of prompts while broad holdout accuracy stays within noise. Random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share help less. Training pivots alone has been hard to stabilize; mixing them into broad RLVR keeps the rest of the policy anchored.

## Setup

- **Start:** [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05), a pure SFT checkpoint. #9933 measured its SWE and Terminal pass rates on this policy, so the selections apply unchanged, and the RLVR data is unseen.
- **RLVR data:** [Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30) (84,403 train / 94 validation rows; 24% single-step tool use, 14% instruction following, 9% code, 13% math, no SWE or Terminal rows). Any SWE or terminal change between arms is therefore attributable to the added turns.
- **Recipe:** the #9735 reference/KL arm (frozen reference, KL 0.01, sequence-mean loss, entropy 0.001, router replay), 512 prompts × 16 samples per step, at most 12 steps, the same seed in every arm. SFT starts in #9735 collapsed after 12 to 20 steps. Asynchronous rollouts with staleness up to 2, TIS correction, a 102,400-token request window with 49,152 tokens per turn, and thinking on, as #9933 measured the pivots' pass rates.
- **RLVR blend as trained:** 63,590 of RLVR1's rows. MarinSkyRL now runs every Nemotron Ultra row as a task session, and code generation, NeMo tool use, NVARC inductive and Lean sessions execute in a Docker task machine that Iris task pods cannot start, so every arm omits those four agents (about 20% of RLVR1, including #9735's code domain). Rows containing a blank text message, which task conversations reject, are dropped too (3,991 RLVR, 59 Terminal). Validation keeps 67 of RLVR1's 94 rows.
- **Pivot prompts:** the runtime drops earlier assistant turns' reasoning from pivot prompts, which #9933's pass-rate measurement kept.
- **Pivots:** #9933's long-format SWE and Terminal candidates, selected at λ = 0.65 (1 to 10 passes of 16) from the pooled K = 16 pass rates already measured on this policy (`users/dml/pivotrl/{swe,terminal}/pass-rates/grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-262k-20261005+seed-1@2026.10.09`). That selects 25,792 of 72,434 scored SWE turns under `nemo` and 6,999 of 36,107 Terminal turns.
- **Reward:** `nemotron_ultra` grades pivot rows through MarinSkyRL#992 with #9933's verifiers: NeMo Gym argument comparison (`nemo`) for SWE and Terminus-2 keystroke similarity without a judge (`string_90`) for Terminal. #10000 uses the same graders. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap the pass rates were sampled at.

## Arms

| Arm | Data |
| --- | --- |
| A | RLVR1 |
| B | RLVR1, with selected pivots replacing 20% of prompts |
| C | RLVR1, with random SWE and Terminal candidate turns replacing 20% of prompts |
| B-10, B-30 (optional) | As B, at 10% and 30% |

The batch stays at 512 prompts, so added turns displace RLVR prompts. Each step carries 102 added turns, 51 SWE and 51 Terminal, because the two benchmarks weigh equally in the decision rules; MarinSkyRL's domain-weighted sampling fills every batch to these counts from route-tagged pools and draws each pool uniformly. RLVR rows come first and their pool is shuffled first, so with one seed B's and C's RLVR prompts are a prefix of A's draw order. Twelve steps use 612 of each pool (25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots), so no turn repeats.

### Why 20%

Only groups with mixed outcomes produce a gradient, and RLVR1 groups already mostly do: `reward/informative_group_fraction` was 0.79 at the first step from the Datakit SFT (Datakit v4, #9735) and fell to about 0.55 by step 12. Resampling the stored K = 16 pass rates, 88% of selected SWE pivots and 81% of selected Terminal pivots come back mixed, against 58% and 24% of random candidate turns. Pivots' share of the gradient is therefore only 1.1 to 1.5 times their share of prompts, and C carries about half of B's pivot signal at the same share.

Pivot-only RL on this SFT, with the same policy learning rate (4e-6) and gradient clip, bounds the dose. One update of 64 SWE pivot groups raised SWE-bench Verified from 26.0% to 29.4% (146 vs 129 of 496 matched tasks, against a historical base run) with AIME24 unchanged; five updates raised held-out pivot accuracy from 0.29 to 0.38. Forty Terminal updates cost 36 points on AIME24 and 9 to 10 on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, and ninety SWE updates collapsed agentic behavior (1 of 248 SWE-bench Verified trials solved, 0 of 190 TBLite) while held-out pivot accuracy kept rising.

Counting a mixed step as its pivot gradient share of a pivot-only update, with RLVR1's informative fraction averaging about 0.68 over the first 12 steps, a first-order approximation that ignores RLVR and KL counteracting drift:

| *p* | Pivot prompts per step | Pivot gradient share | Equivalent pivot-only updates by step 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10% | 51 | ~12% | ~1.5 |
| 20% | 102 | ~24% | ~2.9 |
| 30% | 154 | ~35% | ~4.2 |

With at most 12 steps, 10% delivers about one pivot-only update, the dose that gained about 3 points on SWE, below what the benchmarks resolve. 20% places the dose in the middle of the range where pivot-only training helped, about 14 times below where it did damage, with RLVR still about three quarters of the gradient. B-10 and B-30 bracket it.

## Measurements

- At steps 0, 4, 8 and 12: pass rate on #9933's held-out validation turns graded in process, broad holdout pass@1 and normalized verifier score, and per-domain reward.
- Per step and per source (RLVR, SWE, Terminal): informative group count and mean response length, so B and C are compared by delivered pivot signal and any pull toward shorter RLVR answers shows up early. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap their pass rates were sampled at, through each pivot row's request; the sequence-mean loss weights them like full RLVR answers.
- At step 0 and each arm's step 4, 8 and 12 checkpoints: full SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0) and OpenThoughts-TBLite (Terminus 2), three runs each, compared per task between arms, plus AIME24, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, the benchmarks pivot-only training hurt.
- Checkpoints are selected by the broad holdout and pivot validation, never by the benchmarks. A paired comparison on 500 SWE tasks has a standard error of about 2 points; on 100 tasks it is about 4.4, too wide for the effects expected here.

## Decision rules

- B beats A on SWE-bench Verified or OpenThoughts-TBLite by more than two paired standard errors, with the broad holdout and the four reasoning benchmarks within noise: pivots help in mixed RLVR. Next, test RL-then-merge against the Campaign 3 merge recipe (#9975).
- B ≈ C: selection does not matter at this share; random turns are enough. B > C partly reflects C's smaller pivot signal, so the logged informative group counts qualify the comparison.
- B beats A on pivot validation only: the verifier reward does not transfer to the benchmarks. Revisit the reward component (`exact`) or the generation cap.
- An arm collapses: report its best checkpoint before the collapse and compare arms only at matched steps.

## Prerequisites

1. Per-agent `pivot_reward`, declared among the Nemotron Ultra session settings: MarinSkyRL#992.
2. Selection artifacts at λ = 0.65 from #9933's stored K = 16 pass rates: built, 25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots.
3. Arm datasets: #10215 builds RLVR1 (`open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30@600262dd`) alone, with the selected pivots, and with every scored candidate turn, each row tagged with its route. Rows move from the retired `skyrl_gym` route to `task_session`, which MarinSkyRL grades Nemotron Ultra rows on since its #879. Validation in every arm is RLVR1's 94 rows plus #9933's 508 held-out SWE and 503 Terminal turns.
4. A two-step smoke run of B on 6 nodes (64 prompts with B's composition, 32K window) confirming that every agent's rows load and grade.

## Links

- PivotRL candidates, pass rates and selection: #9933; SFT baselines on the same pivots: #10000; TaskSpec versions of the candidates: #10181
- Prior broad-domain RLVR: #9359, #9735
- Paper: [PivotRL (arXiv 2603.21383)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383)

| 8 | A | +6.2 ★ | +0.8 ★ | −0.2 | +1.0 | −5.0 |
| 8 | B | +7.4 ★ | +0.4 | 0.0 | −3.0 | −2.0 |
| 8 | C | +6.1 ★ | +0.4 | −1.0 | 0.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | A | +5.7 ★ | −1.6 ★ | −7.6 ★ | −4.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | B | +6.6 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.2 (p=.052) | 0.0 | −3.0 |
| 12 | C | +4.5 ★ | −3.4 ★ | −7.8 ★ | −0.3 | −3.0 |

REF accuracies: GPQA-Diamond .635 (n=198), MMLU-Pro .780 (n=12032), Math500 .968 (n=500), AIME24 .830 (n=30), OT-TBLite .16 (n=100). At step 12 B beats A by +5.4 and C by +5.6 on Math500 (both p<.0001) and C by +2.3 on MMLU-Pro (p<.0001). No arm differs from another on GPQA-Diamond or AIME24 at any step, and TBLite with 100 tasks cannot resolve differences under about 9 points.

## Reading

Random turns are the control that makes the SWE-bench result interpretable. C uses the same turn sources, verifiers and share as B, and on the held-out pivot turns it learns the pivot task as fast as B: SWE pivot pass@1 rises from .24 to .42 in both arms and Terminal from .15 to .23, while A stays at .23. Only the selected turns transfer to the benchmark. Random turns also carry less signal, as the plan anticipated: informative-group fraction 0.59 against 0.67 for A and B, and pivot rewards about half of B's.

The GPQA gain of 4 to 8 points in every arm from step 4 comes from the RLVR mix.

The step-12 losses are on hard multi-step items. On Math500, levels 1 to 3 move within 3 points in every arm; level 4 drops 7.8 (A), 2.3 (B) and 8.6 (C) points and level 5 drops 17.2, 4.5 and 15.7. On MMLU-Pro, which is decoded greedily, the losses sit in engineering, chemistry, physics and math; B12 is flat on engineering where A12 is −5.8 and C12 −7.7. The lost Math500 answers run 4.3 times the length of REF's answer to the same question and 34 of A12's 42 end in an extracted wrong answer rather than a truncation. The share of Math500 responses over 100K characters is 0.4% for REF, 4.8% for A4, 8.2% for B12, 11.0% for C12 and 12.4% for A12.

The training curves carry the same signature. Policy entropy rises every step (A 0.83 to 2.76, B to 1.95, C to 2.18) and KL to the frozen reference climbs with no plateau (A .071, B .063, C .086 at step 12), so the 0.01 KL coefficient does not hold the policy. The arm that drifts least degrades least. The in-distribution holdout improves monotonically in every arm (A .21 to .40), so it cannot see the drift; the reference/KL run in #9735 shows the same entropy rise (1.0 to 2.2 by step 10) and had only that holdout. Length stops stay under 9% throughout training and are not the cause.

A's agentic behaviour drifts the same way. Its replies on the pivot validation turns grow 1.5 to 2 times by step 12, A8 overflows the 73K-token context in 17% of SWE-bench tasks (every non-zero agent exit in A8 and A12 is a context-window overflow), and in the A12 eval the median model call took 17 s against 3.6 s for the other runs: 171 of 500 trials hit the 30-minute agent budget, 122 of them then timing out in the verifier. Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors, and the retries have moved A12 from .244 to .272 so far.

## Decision rules

The first rule, B above A on SWE-bench Verified by more than two paired standard errors with the reasoning benchmarks within noise, holds at steps 4 and 8 (SE about 2 points; B−A +6.0 and +9.2). At step 12 no arm has the reasoning benchmarks within noise. The second rule, B ≈ C, fails at every step by 6 to 12 points, and the logged informative-group counts attribute part of that to C's weaker signal. Confidence is limited by one seed per arm; the B effects are 3 to 5 standard errors on SWE-bench, and isolated p<.05 cells such as B8 vs A8 on AIME24 (−4.0, p=.04) are what a hundred comparisons produce.

## What it took

- Layout: 16 H100 nodes per arm, 10 policy nodes with the colocated reference and 12 inference engines at DP4/EP4 on the other 6; 11 to 16 hours per 12-step run.
- Runtime: MarinSkyRL branch `dml/mixed-rlvr-runtime` at bfef1308, seven commits over the fork's main at 563658e5: verifyit pivot graders for the Nemotron pivot rows, per-agent `pivot_reward`, the SWE pivot agent name, null message fields in Parquet prompts, request tools passed as chat tools, and a retry for vLLM engine gangs that die during startup. marin-community/MarinSkyRL#992 carries the first six. The fork was archived on 2026-10-20, so these need porting into `vendor/skyrl` once the verifyit graders from #10215 are published.
- Evaluation: the October 5 verified paired-eval stack (`held/eval-october17-verified` at f9990d36) plus fixes on branch `dml/eval-october17-verified-pivot-mixed-rlvr`: a localhost relay that reports the Iris proxy's 404 during an inference-server reschedule as 503 for ten minutes so Evalchemy retries; Daytona verifier thread limits, because native test libraries sized their pools to the host and exhausted the 300 s verifier timeout; mini-swe-agent pinned to litellm 1.105.1 after an MCP import regression; a 24 h placement budget that treats Kueue's SchedulingGated state as unplaced; the Run:ai streamer load format for staged HF exports; `--cluster-config` so evaluations submit as the openathena.ai login after the contractor service account's default budget demoted jobs to batch band; and an export barrier that waits for the HF export job and verifies its shards before evaluating.
- Scoring: strict first-trial SWE-bench with the fullest run per arm and step; TBLite majority of 3 trials; repeated-trial benchmarks averaged per question.

## Next

- Final A12 SWE-bench number when the retry wave ends.
- A seed-43 replicate of all three arms launched 2026-10-20 21:29 UTC as the openathena.ai login, A on cw-us-east-02a, B and C on cw-rno2a: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/5thdcjv5), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/v8o72kqn), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/2rjy7l3n). C has been preempted three times by production-band jobs on rno2a and restarts from scratch each time.
- The recipe needs a drift fix before running past 8 steps: a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, dropping the entropy bonus, or a length penalty. The optional p arms (B-10, B-30) remain open; the second seed was prioritized.

🤖 Final A12 SWE-bench number: .282, 141 of 500 solved. Harbor's retries of the verifier timeouts finished at 07:47 UTC with every trial scored, so the provisional .272 above becomes .282 and the step-12 row of the SWE-bench table reads A .282, B .308, C .244: B vs A +2.6 (p=.21), B vs C +6.4 (p=.002), C vs A −3.8 (p=.048), B vs REF +4.8 (p=.025), A vs REF +2.2 (p=.28). Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors; the retry wave, run at 16 trials at a time instead of the first pass's full concurrency, scored all of them and lifted A12 by 3.8 points. Those timeouts were therefore partly load-induced rather than a property of the policy, although A12's agents still ran about five times slower per model call than the other arms and overflowed the 73K context in 40 tasks. The step-12 reading changes from B ahead of A by 6 points to B ahead by 2.6 points, not significant; B's lead over A at steps 4 and 8 (+6.0, +9.2) and over C at every step is unaffected, and A's own SWE-bench trajectory is flat (A12 vs A4 −0.6, p=.81).

Seed-43 replicate: all three arms finished 12 steps (B at 08:08 UTC, A and C at about 13:55 UTC; C restarted three times after production-band preemptions on cw-rno2a). C's step-4 checkpoint was pruned by the trainer before its export request landed, so the replicate has no C step-4 point. The two-seed results will follow when those 48 evaluations finish.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Seed-43 replicate, interim. Same recipe, data and evaluation stack as the seed-42 series above, with the run, trainer and data-sampling seeds all set to 43. A trained on cw-us-east-02a and B and C on cw-rno2a, an incidental placement difference (seed 42 had A on rno2a and B and C on us-east) that does not touch the configuration. Training runs: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/5thdcjv5), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/v8o72kqn), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/2rjy7l3n). The trainer pruned C's step-4 checkpoint before its export request landed, so C has no step-4 point and the replicate has 48 evaluations (8 checkpoints × 6 benchmarks). Of those, 32 are complete: steps 4 and 8 on every benchmark except MMLU-Pro and B's OT-TBLite; at step 12 GPQA-Diamond, Math500 and AIME24 for all arms and MMLU-Pro and OT-TBLite for A and C. SWE-bench Verified at step 12, B's OT-TBLite and five MMLU-Pro cells are still running.

B above C on SWE-bench Verified and C below REF replicate. B above A appears at step 8 at a third of the seed-42 size (+3.0, not significant on its own, significant pooled over both seeds) and does not appear at step 4. Every arm again loses Math500 by step 12, and the arm that loses most is the one with the highest step-12 policy entropy: A at seed 42, B at seed 43.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring as above: each seed-43 cell is one complete 500-task run, p-values are exact McNemar tests on the discordant pairs, and the pooled rows sum the discordant pairs of both seeds.

| Step | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | C vs A | B vs REF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4, seed 43 | .260 | .302 | .298 | — | −0.4, p=.93 | — | — | +3.8, p=.087 |
| 8, seed 43 | .260 | .298 | .328 | .202 | +3.0, p=.18 | +12.6, p<.0001 | −9.6, p<.0001 | +6.8, p=.002 |
| 4, both seeds | | | | | +2.8, p=.069 | | | +6.3, p=.0001 |
| 8, both seeds | | | | | +6.1, p=.0001 | +11.3, p<.0001 | −5.3, p=.0001 | +7.9, p<.0001 |

A is above REF at seed 43 (+4.2 at step 4, p=.055; +3.8 at step 8, p=.073) against +2.8 (p=.18) and −0.4 at seed 42; pooled, A vs REF is +3.4 at step 4 (p=.02) and +1.9 at step 8 (p=.21). The step-12 runs have graded 480 of 500 tasks for B (128 solved, .267), 414 for A (140 solved, .338) and 426 for C (143 solved, .336). The three graded sets differ, and the unfinished tasks are the long ones that mostly fail, so these rates are upper bounds for each arm and not comparable across arms. B's step-12 score at seed 42 was .308.

## Other benchmarks, seed 43

Δ vs REF in points. GPQA-Diamond averages 3 samples per question and AIME24 10, tested with a paired sign-flip permutation test; Math500 and MMLU-Pro use exact McNemar; OT-TBLite counts a task solved when at least 2 of 3 trials score 1. One evaluation run per cell. Starred cells have p<.05; "pending" marks a run that is still in progress or being re-run.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +4.4 | +0.7 ★ | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 4 | B | +5.9 ★ | pending | −1.6 | +0.3 | pending |
| 8 | A | +1.2 | pending | −0.8 | −4.3 ★ | −4.0 |
| 8 | B | +9.6 ★ | pending | −0.6 | −2.3 | pending |
| 8 | C | +5.1 ★ | pending | 0.0 | −1.0 | −5.0 |
| 12 | A | −0.3 | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | −2.3 | −8.0 ★ |
| 12 | B | +5.6 ★ | pending | −5.8 ★ | −2.3 | pending |
| 12 | C | +5.9 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | 0.0 | −7.0 ★ |

Arm against arm at seed 43: on GPQA-Diamond B is above A by +8.4 at step 8 (p=.0002) and +5.9 at step 12 (p=.008), and C is above A by +6.2 at step 12 (p=.005); A's GPQA gain fades from +4.4 at step 4 to −0.3 at step 12, where it held at +5.7 at seed 42. On Math500 at step 12, B is below A by 3.0 (p=.02) and below C by 3.0 (p=.036); at seed 42 B was above both by about 5.5. B's OT-TBLite runs lost trials to preemption and are re-running, because the score needs 3 trials per task.

## Reading

Policy entropy at step 12, in nats per token as logged by the trainer, is A 2.11, B 2.53, C 2.23 at seed 43 against A 2.76, B 1.95, C 2.18 at seed 42; KL to the frozen reference policy is A .062, B .071, C .057 against .071, .063, .086. In both seeds the arm with the highest entropy loses the most on Math500 and the arm with the lowest loses the least, and the order of the arms reverses between seeds. Two seeds cannot separate a seed effect from an arm effect, but B's smaller step-12 erosion at seed 42 does not replicate, so it is not a property of the selected-pivot mix. The step-8 checkpoint remains the one to report.

The first decision rule from the plan, B above A on SWE-bench Verified by more than two paired standard errors with no loss on the reasoning benchmarks, holds at step 8 when the two seeds are pooled (+6.1, standard error about 1.5) and does not hold at seed 43 alone (+3.0, standard error 2.1); B shows no reasoning loss relative to A at step 8 (GPQA +8.4, Math500 +0.2, AIME24 +2.0). The second rule, B ≈ C, which would have attributed B's gain to the turn format instead of the selection, fails again by 12.6 points at step 8. Confidence: B above C and C below REF are consistent across both seeds; B above A rests on two seeds with step-8 effects of 3 and 9 points, so its size is uncertain; the GPQA differences between arms come from one run per cell with 198 questions and are suggestive only.

## What it took

- 28 of the 48 evaluations failed on 2026-10-21. CoreWeave object storage answered writes from cw-rno2a with "Account is write suspended for this availability zone", uploads timed out on both clusters, and the Iris controllers stopped answering in-cluster RPCs from about 17:10 UTC on cw-rno2a and 18:27 on cw-us-east-02a; the evaluations failed as their retry budgets ran out between 17:47 and 19:15. All 28 were re-run on cw-us-east-02a.
- From 20:00 UTC on 2026-10-21 the controllers refuse submissions from clients whose lib/iris is more than 14 days old. The October-5 verified evaluation stack is a frozen checkout whose lib/iris was last changed on 2026-10-06, so submissions now go through a side worktree that takes lib/iris and lib/rigging from 2026-10-13 and changes nothing under lib/marin; the evaluation code and results are unaffected.
- Since 01:12 UTC on 2026-10-22, production-band (higher-priority) jobs on cw-us-east-02a have preempted our interactive-band inference servers in six waves. SWE-bench Verified and OT-TBLite run under Harbor, which resumes its job directory and keeps completed trials; the other four benchmarks run under Evalchemy, which restarts from scratch, so the five pending MMLU-Pro cells (A step 8, B steps 4, 8 and 12, C step 8) each need an uninterrupted stretch of 7 to 9 hours.

## Next

- Step-12 SWE-bench Verified and OT-TBLite and the remaining MMLU-Pro cells for seed 43, then the pooled step-12 tests and the two-seed plots.
- The recipe still needs a change that holds the policy near the reference before running past 8 steps (a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, no entropy bonus, or a length penalty); the optional arms that vary the pivot share (B-10, B-30) remain open.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Seed-43 replicate, final. 45 of the 48 seed-43 evaluations are complete. The three missing cells are MMLU-Pro for A at step 8 and B at steps 4 and 8. Their Evalchemy runs need about 9 uninterrupted hours of inference, and production-band preemptions on cw-us-east-02a restarted them every 45 to 60 minutes, so we stopped at 45. C has no step-4 checkpoint at seed 43, as noted in the interim comment. The seed-42 series is complete (54 of 54).

The step-8 checkpoint of B is the result to report. It is the best SWE-bench Verified checkpoint at both seeds, it beats random turns (C) by 10 to 13 points at both seeds, and it costs nothing on the reasoning benchmarks. B's lead over plain RLVR (A) at step 8 is positive at both seeds, +9.2 and +3.0, so its size is uncertain. By step 12 the arms no longer separate on SWE-bench Verified, and every arm loses Math500 and MMLU-Pro against the SFT.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring: first trial per task, an ungraded trial counts as unsolved, 500 tasks per run. p-values are exact McNemar tests. The pooled rows sum discordant pairs over both seeds.

| Step | Seed | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | C vs A |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 42 | .260 | .288 | .348 | .232 | +6.0, p=.004 | +11.6, p<.0001 | −5.6, p=.007 |
| 4 | 43 | .260 | .302 | .298 | — | −0.4, p=.93 | — | — |
| 4 | pooled | | | | | +2.8, p=.069 | | |
| 8 | 42 | .260 | .256 | .348 | .248 | +9.2, p<.0001 | +10.0, p<.0001 | −0.8, p=.74 |
| 8 | 43 | .260 | .298 | .328 | .202 | +3.0, p=.18 | +12.6, p<.0001 | −9.6, p<.0001 |
| 8 | pooled | | | | | +6.1, p<.0001 | +11.3, p<.0001 | −5.2, p=.0001 |
| 12 | 42 | .260 | .282 | .308 | .244 | +2.6, p=.21 | +6.4, p=.002 | −3.8, p=.048 |
| 12 | 43 | .260 | .324 | .260 | .308 | −6.4, p=.001 | −4.8, p=.020 | −1.6, p=.46 |
| 12 | pooled | | | | | −1.9, p=.19 | +0.8, p=.62 | −2.7, p=.048 |

The pooled tests hold the checkpoints fixed and test only item-level noise. They do not account for variation between training seeds, and two seeds cannot estimate that variation. A repeat evaluation of seed-42 B step 8 scored .328 against the original .348: 102 tasks flipped (56 to 46), p=.37. That is the same size as the difference between B's step-8 checkpoints at the two seeds (122 flips, −2.0), so B at step 8 reproduces across seeds within evaluation noise. Seed-42 B vs A at step 8 has 110 discordant tasks split 78 to 32, well outside that noise. Repeats of A at steps 4 and 8 and B at step 4 are still running and will be added here.

## Other benchmarks, seed 43

Δ vs REF in points, with the same tests and conventions as the interim comment. Starred cells have p<.05.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +4.4 | +0.7 ★ | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 4 | B | +5.9 ★ | missing | −1.6 | +0.3 | +1.0 |
| 8 | A | +1.2 | missing | −0.8 | −4.3 ★ | −4.0 |
| 8 | B | +9.6 ★ | missing | −0.6 | −2.3 | +1.0 |
| 8 | C | +5.1 ★ | +0.4 | 0.0 | −1.0 | −5.0 |
| 12 | A | −0.3 | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | −2.3 | −8.0 ★ |
| 12 | B | +5.6 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −5.8 ★ | −2.3 | 0.0 |
| 12 | C | +5.9 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.8 ★ | 0.0 | −7.0 ★ |

On OT-TBLite, B stays within 2 points of REF at both seeds through step 8, while A and C fall 4 to 5 points by step 8. At step 12 it leads A by 8 points at seed 43 (p=.057) and by 1 point at seed 42. With 100 tasks, no OT-TBLite difference between arms is significant on its own. In B's step-12 OT-TBLite run, 13 trials across 10 tasks ended in Daytona sandbox validation errors before Harbor's error gate stopped the job. They count as failed trials, so that score is a lower bound.

## Did the two seeds draw different pivots?

The data-sampling seed changes which pivots B sees, and the two draws share 16 of 612 SWE pivots. Their difficulty is the same. The mean K = 16 pass count of the drawn SWE pivots is 5.22 at seed 42 and 5.26 at seed 43 (chi-square p=.69). For a sample of the Terminal pivots it is 4.00 and 4.04 (Mann-Whitney p=.93). Neither draw contains a SWE-bench Verified repository. The SWE draw was replayed from the sampler and matched the rollout payloads exactly (116 of 116 at the right step). The smaller step-8 gain at seed 43 is not explained by easier or harder pivots.

## Conclusions

- **Selection matters.** B beats C at step 8 at both seeds, by 10.0 and 12.6 points. C is at or below REF at every seed-42 checkpoint and at seed-43 step 8. This is the clearest result of the experiment.
- **Selected pivots help SWE-bench Verified at step 8.** B is above REF by 8.8 and 6.8 points, and above A by 9.2 and 3.0. The first decision rule from the plan, B above A by more than two paired standard errors with no reasoning loss, holds pooled and at seed 42, but not at seed 43 alone.
- **Reasoning benchmarks are not hurt at step 8.** GPQA-Diamond is up for every arm at both seeds. Math500 and MMLU-Pro stay within about a point of REF through step 8. The one significant step-8 loss is A's AIME24 at seed 43, −4.3 points.
- **Every arm drifts by step 12.** Math500 falls 2 to 8 points and MMLU-Pro about 1 to 3 points in all six step-12 runs. SWE-bench rankings at step 12 flip between seeds. The arm that loses most Math500 is the one with the highest policy entropy at step 12, A at seed 42 and B at seed 43.

## Next

- Add the remaining repeat evaluations to the noise estimate above.
- Run past step 8 only with a change that holds the policy near the reference: a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, no entropy bonus, or a length penalty. The optional B-10 and B-30 arms were not run.

Data: the final collection and plots, with series a, b, c, a-seed43, b-seed43, c-seed43, were produced with `experiments/post_training/pivotrl/mixed_rlvr_analysis.py` from #10411 (`collect`, then `plot --shared-items` and `test`).
