comments.body:
🤖 Repeat evaluations, to separate evaluation noise from training-seed variation on SWE-bench Verified. We re-ran SWE-bench Verified on the seed-42 A and B checkpoints at steps 4 and 8. Each repeat used the same checkpoint, harness and strict scoring as the original run. Everything else in the final comment above stands.

| Checkpoint | Original | Repeat | Discordant tasks | Δ | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A step 4 | .288 | .262 | 77 (45 / 32) | −2.6 | .17 |
| A step 8 | .256 | .242 | 83 (45 / 38) | −1.4 | .51 |
| B step 4 | .348 | .340 | 114 (59 / 55) | −0.8 | .78 |
| B step 8 | .348 | .328 | 102 (56 / 46) | −2.0 | .37 |

Rerunning a fixed checkpoint flips 77 to 114 of the 500 tasks and moves the score by up to 2.6 points. Each eval run has a noise standard deviation of roughly 1.4 points. All four repeats came in slightly lower than the originals, by 1.7 points on average. None of the four differences is significant, but the shared direction could come from heavier cluster load during the repeats.

Seed-42 and seed-43 checkpoints of the same arm and step disagree on 91 to 133 tasks. That is somewhat more than the repeats, so the training seed adds variance beyond evaluation noise, mostly at B step 4 (133 discordant, −5.0, p=.037).

B's advantage over A survives re-evaluation:

| Step | B − A, original runs | B − A, repeat runs |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | +6.0 (66 / 36), p=.004 | +7.8 (67 / 28), p<.001 |
| 8 | +9.2 (78 / 32), p<.0001 | +8.6 (76 / 33), p<.0001 |

At seed 42, B's lead over A is a property of the checkpoints and not of one lucky eval run. The seed-43 gaps are smaller, −0.4 at step 4 and +3.0 at step 8. That shortfall comes from training-seed variation, not from evaluation noise. The step-8 conclusion is unchanged: B beats A at both seeds, by an uncertain margin of about 3 to 9 points.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Summary figure and an index of the code, training runs and artifacts behind the two-seed series. The numbers, tests and interpretation are in the [final comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6357439611) and the [repeat-evaluation comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6359491389).

![Checkpoints of three RL arms from the Oct 5 SFT](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d232d289b6c50c376d7ebe97ef18cb95ed4e4d76/experiments/post_training/pivotrl/figures/mixed_rlvr_checkpoints.png)

Each mark is one checkpoint, labelled by its RL step, in its arm's colour; the two marks of one colour and number are the two training seeds. The x-axis is the SWE-bench Verified change against the SFT, the y-axis is the Math500, MMLU-Pro or GPQA-Diamond change, and the cross is the typical ±1 standard error of a mark. B's steps 4 and 8 sit furthest right at no cost on Math500 or MMLU-Pro, C's sit left of zero, every arm's step 12 sits below its steps 4 and 8 on Math500 and MMLU-Pro, and GPQA-Diamond is up for every arm.

The same data as a lookup grid, every checkpoint against every benchmark, with the colour showing the change in standard errors:

![Every checkpoint against every benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d232d289b6c50c376d7ebe97ef18cb95ed4e4d76/experiments/post_training/pivotrl/figures/mixed_rlvr_delta_grid.png)

## Code

issues.body:
The [public Snowball model family tree](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/d3b5517a-c119-4fd9-999d-362183422bf3/v/6/) has been on main since commit 55dd5cc892 ([#9737](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9737), 2026-10-19). Its source is `infra/marina/applets/snowball_family_tree/`. [The documentation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/references/snowball-family-tree.md) describes adding models to `graph-data.json` by PR. Make that the only route, with main as the tree's single source of truth.

Every model addition or edge change should be a reviewed PR to `graph-data.json` on main. Each node should carry its `source` and `evidence` links, and inferred lineage should remain marked `inferred`. Changes should not be sent as files outside the repo.

Releases should come only from main. Run `marina release ... --base-version CURRENT_VERSION` from a clean checkout at the current remote main, as the documentation describes. The release records the git commit. If the live version differs from main, record the difference and its reason in this issue or in the PR that will close the gap. Each tree PR should state whether it needs a release; merging alone does not publish.

As checked on 2026-10-23, live v6's embedded graph data matches main's `graph-data.json`: 130 nodes, 138 edges, snapshot 2026-10-19. Its `app.js` and `style.css` match #9737's second-to-last commit, d33f3101a9. Main includes the final refactor, b41de53442 ("Unify lineage edge markup and remove overridden styles"), which adds an `edgePath()` helper and removes overridden `.edge` CSS rules. That refactor should not change what the tree shows. `index.html` matches once the data is substituted as `build.py` does it.

Earlier versions contain these snapshots: v2/v3, 2026-10-04 with 118 nodes; v4/v5, 2026-10-12 with 126 nodes; and v6, 2026-10-19. Their frontend files match commits on the #9737 branch. There is no data drift to fix today. The proposed process would keep the data aligned as more models arrive.

About 25 SFT-shootout runs trained from Snowball v0 and v0.1 are coming soon, most without published weights. They would be added in one reviewed PR with `model: null` where no public weights exist.

@penfever, does this match your intent for the tree? Should outside contributors' additions also come as PRs, from a fork or opened on their behalf, instead of being folded into a release by hand? Should releases follow every merged tree PR or happen in batches?

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
Fix Pi timeout and cancellation handling in Marin's vendored Harbor runtime. Stop Pi and its child processes before verification starts, so verifier commands can run in the same Daytona session without waiting for leftover agent work.

The [Harbor investigation](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/261) includes a no-model reproduction of this mechanism. A [two-task Luna BixBench smoke](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/261#issuecomment-6372492452) reached the 1,800-second agent limit and then the 300-second verifier limit on both tasks, leaving both ungraded. [Saved Ben and Will evaluation attempts](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/261#issuecomment-6372692406) show the same timing pattern across Pi 1.3.0 and 1.4.0. Historical live process state was not captured, so the mechanism is not proven for every failed attempt.

Ben previously diagnosed remote commands surviving cancellation in [Harbor #13](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/13). The merged [OpenCode fix, #40](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/40), added a remote deadline and OpenCode-specific cleanup. That cleanup does not terminate Pi.

The fix belongs in Marin's vendored runtime: `vendor/harbor/src/harbor/agents/installed/pi.py` and, if needed, `vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona/environment.py`. Scope this issue to Pi on Daytona; a redesign of cancellation across all agents and providers is separate work.

Done when:

- Pi and its child processes stop on agent timeout or cancellation before verification begins; the persistent Daytona session remains usable.
- Regression coverage exercises timeout, explicit cancellation, and ordinary completion, including a child process that would otherwise write after the deadline.
- A bounded live Daytona probe exercises the vendored Pi execution path using a no-model test executable that spawns a child process. Trigger timeout and explicit cancellation through Harbor, without directly killing the test processes. Verify that neither process survives or writes afterward and that a verifier command completes in the same session. Preserve the logs and clean up the sandbox; no model or judge calls are required.
- Timeout classification and grading behavior remain consistent with Harbor's agent-timeout handling; benchmark time budgets are unchanged.

Evaluation adoption should use a merged Marin revision recorded in the run provenance. Historical results remain unchanged.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`Trial._await_phase()` cancels Pi's local task at the agent deadline, but Daytona submits its shell with `run_async=True`, so cancelling the poll does not stop the remote command. Pi launches `pi | node | tee` without a remote deadline, and Daytona's cancellation cleanup targets only `opencode`. This is consistent with the [no-model Harbor reproduction](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/261); the historical failed runs did not capture live process state.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial.py#L515-L594`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3bf0d7a1beaae9351f194ea41eb8f44a9421e945/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L515-L594) — agent deadline and cancellation.
- [`pi.py#L658-L699`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3bf0d7a1beaae9351f194ea41eb8f44a9421e945/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/agents/installed/pi.py#L658-L699) — Pi pipeline without remote deadline.
- [`environment.py#L1941-L2027`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3bf0d7a1beaae9351f194ea41eb8f44a9421e945/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona/environment.py#L1941-L2027) — detached exec and OpenCode-only reap.
- [`trial.py#L715-L741`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3bf0d7a1beaae9351f194ea41eb8f44a9421e945/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L715-L741) — verifier uses the same environment.

# Proposed Fix

1. Isolate each Pi run in a uniquely identified remote process group. Apply a Daytona-side deadline from `environment.agent_timeout_sec` with bounded TERM and KILL of the group and its children; classify a deadline exit as `AgentTimeoutError` without changing the configured agent or verifier budgets.
2. On explicit cancellation or local timeout, terminate that exact Pi process tree through a separate, bounded Daytona control session. Cover cancellation during command submission as well as polling. Wait for confirmed exit before verification; if cleanup cannot be confirmed, fail the trial and retain diagnostics instead of grading alongside a live agent.
3. Add behavior tests in `test_pi.py` with a no-model executable that spawns a delayed-writing child. Cover normal completion, timeout, and explicit cancellation; add Daytona session tests for cleanup and the verifier's ability to execute afterward.
4. Run a bounded live Daytona probe through Harbor's vendored Pi path. Trigger timeout and cancellation, check that neither Pi nor its child survives or writes after the deadline, run a verifier command in the same session, save logs, and delete the sandbox. Daytona credentials are absent from this session, so this gate needs a credentialed runner.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Implementing this in Marin; the PR will remain draft. The current working change gives each Pi invocation a unique supervisor/control directory and uses a separate Daytona session for cancellation. Pi can launch tools in detached process groups, so the supervisor walks and stops the descendant process tree, including a detached child that ignores TERM, before killing it.

The Pi and Daytona test files currently pass (183 tests). New behavior coverage runs the vendored Pi/Daytona execution path against a local SDK-boundary fake with real subprocesses and a per-session queue: deadline, explicit cancellation during polling, normal completion, and subsequent verifier execution.

Your submission-cancellation and cleanup-failure requirements are still being addressed. In particular, `Trial._await_phase()` currently converts exceptions raised during timeout cleanup into the original `AgentTimeoutError`; a failed remote cleanup must remain a fatal infrastructure error so verification cannot proceed. The bounded live Daytona probe is also pending. No evaluation rerun has been launched.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Addressed in draft PR #10612. Cancellation during submission and polling now runs scoped cleanup in a separate Daytona session. If cleanup fails or cannot be confirmed within its bound, `PhaseCancellationError` remains fatal and verification does not proceed.

The final targeted suite passes 203 tests; the full Harbor offline runner passes 1,046 tests after rebasing onto main. A live no-model probe through vendored `Pi.run` and Daytona's session path passed all three cases: remote deadline (`AgentTimeoutError`, 5.28 seconds), explicit cancellation (`CancelledError`, 2.46 seconds), and normal completion (1.44 seconds). The timeout/cancellation cases checked Pi and a detached, TERM-ignoring child were gone or exited, with no delayed output; all cases then ran `verifier-ready` in the same session. The probe used a fake Pi executable and mapped the log file to a writable temporary path. Sandbox deletion was verified.

The supervisor stops parents before enumerating and killing descendants, since Pi tools can create their own process groups. This uses Linux `/proc`; it is not containment for processes that deliberately reparent themselves. No model calls or benchmark reruns were made. The PR remains draft.

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
Add three selected public text-only subsets of [LAB-Bench v1](https://openathena.ai/bio-evals/benchmarks/lab-bench) to Marin's vendored Evalchemy and expose each component separately in EvalDash. This prepares LAB-Bench for a proposed in-distribution (ID) development evaluation under the [Marin evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Canonical policy adoption remains a separate decision after validation.

Scope:

| Component | Public questions | Evaluation key |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| ProtocolQA | 108 | `lab-bench-protocolqa` |
| SeqQA | 600 | `lab-bench-seqqa` |
| CloningScenarios | 33 | `lab-bench-cloning` |

Use all 741 public questions from a pinned [dataset revision](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench). The model receives text and generates a multiple-choice answer without browsing, code execution, or other external tools. SeqQA therefore measures unaided sequence reasoning.

Open policy discussion: runtime and subset size. Measure evaluator wall-clock time for each component, excluding scheduler wait and model-server startup, and record model, reasoning/output limits, concurrency and timeout settings. Report mean runtime and sample standard deviation across the evaluated model cohort, following the [evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197); distinguish small-smoke timings from full-benchmark measurements. The policy's 30-minute Evalchemy trial limit is separate from the overall job timeout; the current exploratory smoke uses 20 minutes per request and a four-hour job limit. Before ID adoption, discuss whether all 741 questions are practical for routine evaluation or whether a fixed, representative subset is needed, preserving separate component scores and SeqQA subtask coverage. Any subset should pin its selection rule and question IDs and report the resulting uncertainty; this remains an open decision, not a scope change to the current integration.

Deferred scope and rationale:

| Item | Why deferred | Requirements for a follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool-enabled versions of the selected subsets, especially SeqQA | Tools change the measured capability from unaided reasoning to performance with an agent and its tools. Establish the no-tools baseline first. | Define a separately named protocol with fixed tools, agent, network access and execution budgets; validate a Harbor task adaptation and retain tool traces. |
| LitQA2 (199), SuppQA (82), DbQA (520) | These target literature, supplementary-material and database retrieval. A no-tools score is possible, but would not establish retrieval capability. | Specify literature/corpus access, supplement handling and database versions or snapshots, plus tool and network policy. Validate source availability and scoring under that protocol. |
| FigQA (181), TableQA (244) | Both supply images, including TableQA's tables. They require a vision-capable evaluation path and model cohort. | Preserve image inputs and validate the multimodal route. Treat the existing Harbor FigQA agent protocol separately from direct tool-free image answering; it does not cover TableQA. |
| LABBench2 | It is a distinct benchmark with different tasks and grading, requiring its own scope and integration assessment. | Review dataset access, subset selection and native evaluators before proposing a separate addition. |
| Authors' private holdout | It is not part of the public release available for this implementation. | Obtain author-approved access and evaluation terms before considering its use. |
| Overall LAB-Bench score and canonical cross-benchmark ranking weight | A pooled score would be dominated by the 600 SeqQA questions; selecting all three columns in current EvalDash rankings gives LAB-Bench three entries. | Agree on canonical aggregation and suite weighting before policy adoption. Keep these entries out of canonical release panels until then; exploratory dashboard selections retain the existing per-column weighting. |

Counts refer to the public [LAB-Bench dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench). These deferrals do not assign the omitted subsets an ID or OOD designation.

Implement one shared loader and prompt builder in `vendor/evalchemy/eval/`, reusing the existing multiple-choice grader, with three task registrations and three Marin evaluation configurations. Register the evaluation keys in `experiments/evaluation/evals.py`; no dedicated launcher suite, dashboard group or benchmark-specific grader is required. Evalchemy's benchmark sources are included in the vendored runtime, so this change belongs in Marin. Harbor's vendored runtime excludes adapter generators; its existing [LAB-Bench adapter](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/main/adapters/labbench) covers FigQA only and is outside this scope.

Separate component scores must be available for model comparisons, not only in a run's metric details. Evalchemy already supports tagged subgroup metrics, and Marin preserves per-task metrics, but [EvalDash's measurement layer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/86fc7b67c9/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/eval_measurements.py#L254) produces one headline measurement per registered evaluation name. Use the three evaluation entries to obtain separate columns, histories and coverage accounting without a dashboard redesign. Preserve finer SeqQA subtask scores and counts as diagnostic metrics.

Protocol deviations and agreed simplifications:

- Use the named variant `marin-labbench-no-tools-v3`. Preserve each dataset question's correct answer and distractors, but do not add the author harness's insufficient-information/abstention choice. This is a forced-choice capability evaluation; it does not reproduce the original uncertainty-calibration evaluation or its historical scores.
- Report accuracy, standard error and sample counts for each component using the existing reducer. Remove abstention-specific precision, attempted-answer coverage and related counters. Infrastructure failures retain the shared execution-error handling and are not interpreted as model abstentions.
- Allow generated reasoning and request a final `Answer: X`, replacing the original tagged-answer format. Reuse Evalchemy's `letter_choice` grader with HLE's extractor rather than adding a LAB-Bench grader. There is no LLM extraction fallback. The shared grader now prefers the provider's final-answer field and strips explicit thinking blocks. Normally completed reasoning-only responses remain eligible for extraction; reasoning-only truncations score zero. Within the selected text, the extractor uses the first answer-prefixed letter, then the last isolated letter as a fallback. This correction follows MMLU-Pro's existing handling and also affects HLE and GPQA Diamond. Version 2 could select an intermediate answer from reasoning; preserve its original results and label any v3 rescoring of saved responses separately from fresh generation.
- Shuffle choices deterministically per item using the run seed, subset and item ID. Pin the dataset, prompt and scoring implementation, and retain the seed and effective run/model settings. This defines reproducible Marin permutations rather than claiming exact reproduction of the author harness.
- Use Evalchemy's existing output-budget resolution and endpoint context checks, with no LAB-Bench-specific fixed output cap or context-overflow-as-abstention rule. Explicit run/model output limits take precedence; otherwise generation uses the context remaining after the measured prompt reserve and shared margins. The checked-in configuration requests one response per item, temperature 0, seed 42 and thinking enabled; record effective overrides for comparisons.

The implementation and protocol are described in [draft PR #10582](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10582) and its benchmark README. Earlier tagged-answer/abstention runs are not comparable to this variant. Tools, omitted components and the overall score remain deferred as listed above.

Partial validation (2026-10-23): the same three questions per component were generated on free GLM-5.3, then all nine preserved responses were rescored offline with the v3 shared grader at `6ae3623e76259a768314a440a4e9e7a43e87447c`. Rescoring made no model calls and preserved the original v2 results.

| Component | Original v2 correct | Corrected v3 correct | Generation/evaluation time | Output-limit truncations |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| ProtocolQA | 2/3 | 2/3 | 13m45s | 1/3 |
| SeqQA | 0/3 | 2/3 | 36m54s | 1/3 |
| CloningScenarios | 0/3 | 0/3 | 40m37s | 3/3 |

All nine responses were durably saved; none failed with a request timeout. The five truncated responses contained reasoning without a final answer. The corrected grader recovered two correct SeqQA final answers that v2 had misread from reasoning. The generation job took 1h32m including setup; the offline rescoring job took 44 seconds including setup. These are three-question smoke timings, not full-component runtime estimates or benchmark scores. All three SeqQA questions belong to one subtask, so this smoke does not establish coverage of every SeqQA subtask. No corrected EvalDash publication is claimed.

Effective generation settings: temperature 0, top_p 1, seed 42, medium reasoning effort, concurrency 1, context 262144, request timeout 1200 seconds, overall job limit 14400 seconds, no automatic model-call retries. Context-derived output ceilings were 256791 / 257360 / 235436 tokens for ProtocolQA / SeqQA / CloningScenarios. Runtime and output-budget practicality remain open policy questions alongside representative subsetting.

Durable evidence: original responses and v2 scores under `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/eval-validation/labbench-10575/glm-context-durable-af5e418160-20261023/results`; separately verified v3 scores under the same parent at `rescoring/6ae3623e76259a768314a440a4e9e7a43e87447c.json`. Generation used commit `af5e4181603ae1e314be703cf778096a6055c7f6`; the rescoring record retains per-response hashes and original/corrected answers. Scripts and the timing/identity audit are archived under the same parent at `rescoring-evidence-6ae3623e76.tar.gz`.

Done when:

- [ ] The pinned public dataset yields the expected component counts and stable item IDs. Correct-choice labels and grading metadata remain hidden; correct answer text appears as an unlabeled member of the shuffled choices.
- [ ] The forced-choice protocol and departures from the author harness are documented. Reuse shared grader/runtime tests and add only focused dataset-adaptation coverage; verify choice/target alignment and verify the corrected final-content extraction on saved responses before accepting baseline scores.
- [ ] Each component runs independently; the existing comma-separated evaluation selector can select all three, without a new suite.
- [ ] A bounded end-to-end smoke run for each component retains prompts, responses, grades and dataset/runtime provenance. Smoke results are identified as partial validation, not full benchmark scores.
- [ ] EvalDash displays three separately comparable evaluations with the correct headline accuracy, item counts and run-detail metrics. SeqQA diagnostic subtask scores survive into the stored records.
- [ ] Documentation records the exact no-tools protocol and remaining requirements for policy adoption. A full scored baseline panel is tracked separately from implementation readiness; canonical release panels remain unchanged until policy adoption resolves component weighting, runtime and any subset selection.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

Marin installs Evalchemy from a pinned external fork; this checkout has no `vendor/evalchemy/eval/`, so the issue's proposed source path cannot run as written. The current EvalDash headline path is `infra/evaldash/src/metrics.py`, which selects one primary metric per evaluation record; three registered evaluation names provide three columns. No open Marin PR matched LAB-Bench or #10575. This session cannot inspect PRs in the Evalchemy fork because its GitHub grant covers Marin only.

**Relevant code**
- [`config/external/README.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/config/external/README.md#L1) — external fork and pin workflow
- [`experiments/evaluation/evals.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L216) — evaluation and suite registry
- [`evalchemy/result.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/result.py#L80) — persisted per-task metrics
- [`evaldash/metrics.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/infra/evaldash/src/metrics.py#L117) — headline rollup by task
- [`finestore/eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L62) — primary metric priority

# Proposed Fix

1. Add one shared LAB-Bench v1 loader, prompt builder, deterministic parser, and grader to `marin-community/evalchemy`, then advance Marin's pinned Evalchemy revision. Pin the public dataset revision; assert 108/600/33 items and stable IDs; shuffle choices with a recorded seed while keeping the correct label and grading metadata out of model prompts. The fork change is a prerequisite to this Marin PR under the current runtime layout.
2. Treat explicit abstention as unattempted. Treat an unparseable non-abstaining response as attempted and incorrect, with a separate parse-failure count. Define accuracy as correct/all scored items, precision as correct/attempted, and attempted-answer coverage as attempted/all scored items; precision is undefined when attempted is zero. Fail an incomplete run on context overflow instead of recording a benchmark score, and document this difference from the authors' abstention convention and Claude 2 fallback.
3. Add three Evalchemy YAML configs and registry keys plus `lab-bench-no-tools` in `experiments/evaluation/evals.py`. Pin shots, repetitions, thinking, sampling, context and output budgets in the protocol record. Emit `accuracy` as each task's headline metric, plus precision, attempted coverage, counts, parse failures, and SeqQA subtask diagnostics. Add the three keys to EvalDash's presentation suite; test that its headline uses the component aggregate and retains diagnostic metrics.
4. Validate the grader against author cases or documented reference cases, including shuffled choices, abstention, malformed output, zero attempts and denominators. Run a bounded smoke evaluation for each component and inspect saved prompts, responses, grades, item counts and provenance in EvalDash. Publish protocol documentation and track a separate full baseline panel; leave canonical release panels unchanged until policy adoption decides weighting.

comments.body:
🤖 The source-layout finding is checkout-dependent: current main includes [vendored Evalchemy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2a75182dbd02eeebcb92fe820829c04465fb2240/vendor/evalchemy/README.md), and the [Harbor vendor guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2a75182dbd02eeebcb92fe820829c04465fb2240/vendor/harbor/README.md) explicitly excludes adapter generators. This implementation targets the vendored Evalchemy source in Marin; a separate fork change and pin bump are not prerequisites.

The three evaluation registrations and separate EvalDash columns remain the plan. Deterministic parsing is agreed: malformed responses count as attempted and incorrect, explicit abstentions remain separate, and parse failures are reported. The pinned author evaluator returns precision 0 when no answers are attempted, so the implementation preserves that convention and reports the attempted-answer count alongside it. Context overflow fails validation before generation for the selected cohort rather than becoming abstention. These parser and overflow differences will be documented as a Marin protocol variant.

Implementation is underway; no live smoke result is available yet. Canonical release panels remain unchanged pending policy adoption and weighting decisions.

🤖 Implemented the three public no-tools components in vendored Evalchemy, with separate Marin keys and EvalDash accuracy columns. Precision, attempted-answer coverage, abstentions, parse failures and SeqQA subtask scores remain attached to each component. The source and grader share one implementation; registration discovery now supports multiple task names per source directory.

The pinned dataset contains 108 ProtocolQA, 600 SeqQA and 33 CloningScenarios items, with distinct IDs and 15 SeqQA subtasks. With the pinned Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer and thinking template, the maximum prompt lengths are 5,099 / 4,530 / 26,454 tokens. The largest prompt requires 34,710 tokens including the 8,192-token output budget and context margin, so the configurations use 40,960. Overflow fails before generation.

The final Iris smoke completed three questions per component, with 9/9 scored and no execution errors. All nine outputs failed the strict tagged-answer parser: each component has accuracy 0, precision 0, attempted-answer coverage 1, abstention rate 0 and parse-failure rate 1. These are partial integration results, not baseline benchmark scores. Correct answers, wrong answers, explicit abstentions and malformed answers are covered by grader tests. All nine prompts, responses, grades and diagnostics were read back through EvalDash; the three columns remain separate. The smoke model is archived, so inspecting it requires including archived models and partial runs.

The smoke group is `20261023-165019-qwen3-0.6b-0109ded502a3442684272136661a60c7`. Model revision: `c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca`; Evalchemy runtime SHA-256: `ab7c9cce3c7ddb467a5c1fc26953227ddf7472e1910fa1f7d31db427e980fc28`. Inference worker and broker shutdown is verified.

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
### Slurm wrapper used by every command in this issue

All commands submit `run_gpu.sh` from `$WORK/marin` on the AMD HPC Fund cluster. It turns XLA command buffers off; a later `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=...` in `XLA_FLAGS` overrides that. It will be committed to the repo; this comment is the reference until then.

<details><summary>run_gpu.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -o pipefail
cd "$WORK/marin"
export RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=${RAGGED_DOT_IMPL:-xla} PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this ROCm stack: nan gradients and segfaults after a few steps.
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer= $XLA_FLAGS"
uv run --no-sync python "$@" 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered -v -E "rocm_pcie_bandwidth|rocm_executor"
```

</details>

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

comments.author: asartran
comments.body:
🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,229 TFLOP/s in JAX by kernel time (53% of datasheet peak, 97% of PyTorch's sustained 1,261)

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421), 6b47d18 (JAX 454529), 370d41d (JAX 454561), 704ceff (JAX 454577-454580) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt and rocBLAS; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |
| Kernel tracing | `rocprofv3` from the `rocm-sdk-core` 10.0.0 wheel |
| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |
| Python, OS | 3.12.12, Linux 5.14.0-611.54.1.el9_7 |
| JAX flags | `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`; the Triton-off run adds `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` |

Each run used GPU 0 while the other 7 GPUs on the node were idle.

```bash
sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/mamf.sbatch --dtype bfloat16"
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/jax_matmul.sbatch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --m-range 4096 20480 4096 --n-range 4096 20480 4096 --k-range 4096 20480 4096 \
  --shapes-file experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK. The JAX column is kernel time, with the traced wall-clock rate of the same shape in parentheses.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,229 (53.3%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,178) | 453328, 454577 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,086 (47.1%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,047) | 453329, 454578 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's projection shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted (job 454579). By kernel time, JAX reaches 97% of MSMF in bf16 and 92% in fp16. Without the tracer, the best bf16 wall-clock rate was 1,192 at 4096x4096x16384 and 1,180 at 4096x4096x12288 (job 453420).

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.3% of the JAX bf16 kernel-time ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has kept the fastest rocBLAS or hipBLASLt solution for that shape; the TunableOp column names the library it picked. JAX kernel time comes from job 454579, where XLA's autotuner picked a hipBLASLt kernel for every shape. JAX wall clock comes from job 453412, which ran without the tracer.

| Shape | MSMF | TunableOp | JAX kernel | JAX / MSMF, kernel | JAX wall | JAX / MSMF, wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | rocBLAS | 1,052 | 83% | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | hipBLASLt | 1,209 | 97% | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | rocBLAS | 1,199 | 97% | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | hipBLASLt | 1,179 | 96% | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | hipBLASLt | 1,111 | 102% | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | rocBLAS | 959 | 89% | 828 | 77% |

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 12% lower by kernel time.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). Treat differences of about 3% as noise. XLA's autotuner can also pick a different hipBLASLt kernel for the same shape in a new run. It did so for 4 of the 28 MAMF shapes between jobs 454579 and 454580 and moved three of them by 7-12% (for example 20480x4096x12288: 1,039 with a 192x320 tile in job 454579, 1,164 with a 256x256 tile in job 454580).
- Under `rocprofv3`, wall clock reads lower for shapes that take less than about 100 µs per call, because the tracer adds host work to every dispatch: 4096x1280x2560 reads 401 traced (job 454561) and 472-550 in two untraced passes (job 454529). Wall-clock numbers above say which kind they are.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004 by wall clock, and faster on 26 of the 28 shapes (jobs 453412 and 453338). The two slower shapes, 20480x4096x12288 (-8%) and 16384x8192x8192 (-4%), may reflect XLA's autotuner picking a different kernel rather than the node: 1,043 on k007-002 matches the 192x320-tile kernel in the variation note, and these two runs did not record kernel names. k007-001 and k007-003 have not been compared. The bf16 grid's best wall-clock rate was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The MI350X MAMF and MSMF runs (jobs 453328 and 453329) predate the fix in stas00/ml-engineering#143, so their power and clock readings, the 38 MHz and 308 W in their logs, and the "not a boost burst" warning from the MAMF boost check all come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86%, JAX by kernel time on the same shape (1,189 in job 454577) about 81%, and JAX by untraced wall clock in job 453523 (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.
- Next: measure a training step with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` to see whether the faster hipBLASLt kernels for the k and v GEMMs carry over. Separately, check whether XLA can use the rocBLAS solutions TunableOp picked for 4608x4096x7168 and 2048x4096x4096 (`tunableop-*.csv` in the results directory), and whether those solutions close the remaining gaps.

</details>

### MI350X Triton `ragged_dot` rewrite and tuning: batch 64 step 2.634 → 2.426 s, 8.58% → 9.32% MFU

Commit: 8471641 (local, not pushed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 453565 (A/B), 453564 (microbenchmark), baseline 453384

PR: #9859 (AMD Instinct only; NVIDIA, TPU and megablox unchanged).

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" \

```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.
- Tuned for MI350X: 256×256×64 tiles, 8 warps, 2 stages for forward and dlhs; 256×128×64, 4 warps, 1 stage for drhs; plus chiplet-aware program order. Blackwell, TPU and megablox are unchanged.
- Per call on one GPU at batch 64 (M=131072), before → after TFLOP/s:

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

  A dense `jnp.matmul` of the same FLOPs runs at about 925–958; XLA fp16 `ragged_dot` at 24–98. At batch 8 the forward pass goes from 2.27 ms to 0.36 ms. Jobs 453500 and 453564.
- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

The model's async EP all-gathers take 4.1 ms (about 280 GB/s) because they share compute units and HBM with concurrent compute: next to a matmul, an all-gather hides only 42% of it, even with the latency-hiding scheduler on.

Exposed time is 402 ms. It also drops more assignments: 5.4% against ring's 0.9% at capacity factor 1.0.

- Next, by estimated upside: `save_moe` at batch 64 now (-3.7%, +49 GiB); token-deduplicated EP dispatch (about 58% fewer EP bytes, 100-180 ms); overlap the synchronous reduce-scatters with the shared-expert MLP (50-100 ms); one gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan (40-55 ms).

</details>

  4. `ragged_dot` drhs and fwd w2 tiles: 55-75 ms

  6. one gradient all-reduce after the scan: 35-45 ms
  7. a Pallas top-k for routing: 30-40 ms
  8. optimizer fusion: 40-55 ms (Adam in the benchmark; production uses MuonH)
  9. launch overhead: at most about 45 ms; skip

  Items 2 and 4-7 are independent and together reach about 1.55-1.62 s (14.0-14.6%).

</details>

🤖 Matmul-alone time in the MI350X `--overlap` runs (jobs 453572, 453633, 453651) takes one of two values between runs: about 2.46 ms in `min64`, `ring`, `prio-on` and `lhs-prio-off`, and about 2.88 ms in the other 16. Details: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9886#issuecomment-6047294744

Because the variance is between processes, re-timing the matmul inside a run does not remove it. To compare settings, run each setting in several processes, interleave them, and compare medians of a per-run ratio such as the hidden fraction `(t_collective + t_matmul − t_both) / min(t_collective, t_matmul)`, using the matmul-alone time of the same run.

### Token-deduplicated EP dispatch (`ring_dedup`): 1.580 s and 14.31% MFU with `save_moe`, -8.7% against ring

Commit: 91286fc (local; `ring_dedup` backend in b31085d, merged onto the gather-combine base 67ca557) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454021 (`ring_dedup`), 454012 (ring baseline)

PR: #9880 (draft, merge after #9860). `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` comes from #9852.

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.580 s | 165,900 | 14.31% | 206.5 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What it does.** `ring` all-gathers every token to all 8 GPUs and reduce-scatters a full-size output, but with top-4 of 256 experts a token reaches only 3.3 GPUs on average. `ring_dedup` (new module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring_dedup.py`) sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`, plus a small `all_to_all` of per-row combine weights and local expert ids. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, grouped layout and Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32 and returns one row per token. All hidden-width movement is a gather (ring's `_dispatch_rows`/`_combine_rows`), so there are no scatter-adds in either pass.
- **Sender capacity** is `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing (0.416 × 32,768 per GPU). At 1.1 it sends 537 MB per collective per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring's all-gather or reduce-scatter (46%), and drops no tokens at the sender in these runs.
- **A/B, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile cache per job, `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, median of steps 2-19:**

  | Base | Remat | ring | `ring_dedup` | Jobs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | merged (gather combine + Triton routing top-k) | recompute_all | 1.798 s, 12.57% | 1.688 s, 13.40% (-6.1%) | 454022, 454026 |
  | merged | save_moe | 1.730 s, 13.07% | 1.580 s, 14.31% (-8.7%) | 454012, 454021 |
  | before the gather combine | recompute_all | 1.865 s, 12.13% | 1.735 s, 13.03% (-7.0%) | 453921, 453922 |
  | before the gather combine | save_moe | 1.842 s, 12.28% | 1.637 s, 13.81% (-11.1%) | 453960, 453968 |

  The two changes stack partly. With `save_moe`, the gather combine alone saves 112 ms, `ring_dedup` alone 205 ms, both together 262 ms. Peak memory changes by at most 0.7 GiB. Step-19 loss is within 8e-4 of ring in every pair. The drop rate is 1.00% vs 0.99% (`recompute_all`) and 1.12% vs 0.93% (`save_moe`).
- **Numerics.** f32 CPU unit tests on 8 shards match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in value and in gradients for x, combine weights and both expert weights, including a forced sender-drop case. At full shapes in bf16 on MI350X, one layer differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative in value and gradients. That comes from ring's bf16 summation; `ring_dedup` sums in f32.
- **Profile (steps 10-12, GPU 0, ms per profiled step, ring vs `ring_dedup`, both before the gather combine).** `recompute_all`: large EP collectives take 481 vs 311, exposed collective time is 357 vs 288, and MoE dispatch/combine kernels take 150 vs 42. `save_moe`: 386 vs 211, 402 vs 266, and 147 vs 40. Each large `all_to_all` takes 1.6-2.7 ms, against 3.3-4.2 ms for ring's collectives.
- **What is still exposed:** the forward return and backward dy `all_to_all`s are synchronous (about 60 ms each per step), and the small metadata `all_to_all`s take 0.8-0.9 ms per call under `save_moe`, where they queue behind the large transfers.
- The latency-hiding scheduler gave 1.594 s vs 1.637 s before the merge, but 1.591 s vs 1.580 s after it (job 454027), so leave it off.
- One run (454010) hit the step-5 GPU-7 out-of-memory on a 96.6 GiB allocation, the same failure seen at batch 96 in job 453660, and hung. The retry (454021) ran clean. Since diagnosed as allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer and fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- **Follow-ups:** packing the metadata into the activation rows and chunking the expert MLP were tried and did not help; see the next comment. Not tested on TPU or NVIDIA.

</details>

| 60b253d | recompute_all | baseline | 1.844 s | 142,200 | 12.26% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.852 s | 141,600 | 12.21% | 158.4 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

</details>

### Hiding `ring_dedup`'s synchronous all-to-alls behind the shared expert: no gain

Commit: 3838b71 (local, on the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454847, 454872, 454943 (overlap + latency-hiding scheduler); 454865, 454945, 454949 (latency-hiding scheduler only); 454857, 454892 (baseline)

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton \
  XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

</details>

- Setup: the 14.31% configuration (flash attention, Triton `ragged_dot`, `ring_dedup` at transport capacity 1.1, `save_moe`) at 8 or 12 sequences per GPU. Step is the median of steps 2-19, with a fresh compile per run. MFU is against the peak of all GPUs in the run.

comments.body:
🤖 ### bf16 XLA grouped GEMM on MI350X: hipBLASLt has no bf16 grouped kernels for gfx950, and its one fp16 grouped kernel is 8-21x slower than Triton

Commit: none (standalone JAX script, no Marin code) · GPU: one MI350X per configuration, run side by side on one node · Job: 460950

```bash
# $WORK/marin/.venv: JAX 0.11.0, jax-rocm10-plugin, ROCm 10.0.0 from pip.
# Command buffers stay off because hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM crashes with them on (#9904).
# Times jax.lax.ragged_dot (fwd) and its VJP (bwd: dlhs and drhs) by wall clock over 20 calls,
# then sums GPU kernel time by kernel name over 5 calls under jax.profiler.
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype bfloat16  # bf16, XLA default
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype float16   # fp16, hipBLASLt grouped GEMM
```

Useful TFLOP/s per call (2·M·K·N per pass, counting only each row's own expert). Shapes are per GPU as in #9859 (w13: fused gate/up projection; w2: down projection), with 32 experts and equal row counts. bwd is dlhs and drhs together. The Triton column is #9859's tile-map kernels at the same shapes (job 457866, from the PR description); for bwd it gives the combined rate, then dlhs / drhs.

| Shape (M, K, N) | Pass | bf16 XLA (default) | fp16 XLA grouped GEMM | bf16 Triton, #9859 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13, batch 64 (131072, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 35.6 | 37.4 | 784 |
| | bwd | 29.5 | 38.9 | 743 (806 / 689) |
| June w2, batch 64 (131072, 1280, 2560) | fwd | 36.6 | 52.9 | 725 |
| | bwd | 27.1 | 38.1 | 696 (764 / 639) |
| June w13, batch 8 (16384, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 36.2 | 36.5 | 621 |
| | bwd | 33.5 | 71.3 | 562 (632 / 506) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **Relaxing XLA's gate is not enough.** XLA lowers `ragged_dot` to hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM only where `CanBeHandledByGpublasltGroupGemm` in `xla/hlo/transforms/expanders/ragged_dot_rewriter.cc` allows it: fp16 and bf16 on gfx942, fp16 only on gfx950 (openxla/xla#38088, unchanged on XLA `main`). The gate follows hipBLASLt's kernel coverage. The gfx950 kernel libraries in hipBLASLt from ROCm 7.1 and 7.2 (the cluster's system installs) and ROCm 10.0 (pip) have grouped-GEMM kernels for fp16 only, and `ROCm/rocm-libraries` `develop` has no bf16 grouped-GEMM tuning logic for gfx950. A plugin rebuilt with the gate relaxed would have no bf16 kernel to call.
- **The gfx950 fp16 grouped GEMM has one kernel.** Each gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM logic file in [`rocm-libraries`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/tree/develop/projects/hipblaslt/library/src/amd_detail/rocblaslt/src/Tensile/Logic/asm_full/gfx950/gfx950/GridBased) (about 9 KB) lists a single solution with a 16x16x32 tile. The gfx942 bf16 grouped-GEMM files list 4-7 MB of tuned solutions per layout. In the profiles, that `MT16x16x32` kernel accounts for the whole fp16 call. bf16 and fp16 matrix-core throughput is the same on gfx950, so a bf16 build of the same kernel would not be faster. XLA's setup kernel (`SetUserArgsKernelRaggedIn*Dim`) takes about 6 µs per GEMM.
- **XLA's default bf16 path does 32x the useful work.** It runs one hipBLASLt matmul of every row against every expert's weights at 1.20-1.42 PFLOP/s, then masks the result. The matmul is 68-91% of the call, and transposes and the mask take the rest. fp16 with `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_grouped_gemm=false` takes the same path at 25-34 TFLOP/s.
- **The possible gain is small.** On MI300X, where hipBLASLt has tuned bf16 grouped kernels, XLA's grouped GEMM took 11-28% less time per call than tuned Triton (#9904, microbenchmarks only). Triton `ragged_dot` was 21% of the MI350X batch-64 step in [this profile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6026123445), taken before the kernel rewrite and flash attention. If the MI300X edge carried over to gfx950, it would save about 2-6% of step time (21% × 11-28%), and less now that the rewritten Triton kernels are faster.
- **If someone picks this up:** test fp16 first, because it needs no plugin rebuild. Generate large-tile gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM solutions from the `rocm-libraries` tag that matches ROCm 10.0.0, and set `HIPBLASLT_TENSILE_LIBPATH` to a copy of the stock gfx950 library directory with the new files added. Add bf16 solutions and rebuild the plugin with the gate relaxed only if fp16 beats Triton. The other route is to ask AMD to ship tuned gfx950 grouped-GEMM kernels in hipBLASLt. Until then, MI350X keeps Triton `ragged_dot`.

</details>

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
Add small structural evals for basic agent behavior. The [BixBench trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found answers left in chat instead of the required file, and simulated tool execution with no actual tool calls. The audit does not isolate model behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior.

Cover four checks:

- Required-file submission: when instructed to write an answer to a path, verify that a nonempty file exists in the actual task environment. An answer in chat or a claimed write does not pass.
- Actual tool execution: verify a real tool invocation and its execution status for tasks that need one. Tool-call markup, invented tool responses, or a narrated shell session do not pass. Distinguish missing/invalid invocations, executor failures/timeouts, and successful execution.
- Thinking disabled: verify the emitted response respects the supported `thinking=false` setting. Define the prohibited reasoning-channel output or delimiters under the pinned template; this checks observable output, not internal reasoning. Keep extraction/serving errors distinguishable from model violations.
- URL loading: when a task explicitly requires information at a supplied URL and a retrieval tool is available, verify an actual retrieval attempt. Record tool/network failures separately from failure to attempt retrieval.

Done when:

- Each check has minimal tasks and positive/negative grader fixtures, including narrated execution and missing-file cases.
- Results separate protocol compliance, submission completeness, and answer correctness. Passing the structural check alone must not imply a correct answer.
- Traces retain the request settings, raw response, parsed tool calls, execution events, and checked artifacts needed to locate failures.

Scope is evaluation additions; training interventions are separate.

Related: #10060 (output-contract validation), #10061 (tool-protocol syntax and localized supervision).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [BixBench audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found 156/205 tasks without the required answer file and a trace that narrated shell execution with no tool event; the evidence does not isolate model output from parsing or execution. Harbor keeps a trajectory but maps verifier reward to one `correct` value, leaving no separate protocol, submission, and answer labels. The duplicate preflight found no PR for these four checks; [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers BFCL training and syntax diagnostics.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L316-L352`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L316-L352) — validates one Harbor dataset and agent.
- [`runner.py#L126-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L126-L145) — reads trial result and trajectory path.
- [`runner.py#L172-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L172-L189) — equates reward with `correct`.
- [`eval.py#L111-L141`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L111-L141) — sample and metric contract.
- [`eval.py#L288-L342`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L288-L342) — flattened trajectory fields.

# Design: agent protocol probes

Add a versioned four-task diagnostic through the evaluation launcher. Pin the model revision, chat template, tool schema/parser, agent/runtime revision, request settings, and task content. Use Harbor's existing local dataset path for sandbox checks; use a dedicated single-turn request to the same served endpoint for `thinking=false`, so the grader can inspect the exact request and response independently of an agent's final message.

1. **Required file.** Ask for a short known answer in `/workspace/answer.txt`. The verifier reads that path in the task environment after the agent stops and records existence, byte count, and content hash. Score file presence separately from matching the known answer; chat text or a claimed write cannot satisfy presence.
2. **Tool execution.** Ask the agent to obtain a per-trial nonce with an exposed shell tool. Record the raw generated response before tool parsing, parsed calls, dispatch/start/end events, and exit status. Label missing or invalid invocation, executor error/timeout, and successful execution separately. A narrated shell session, tool-call markup in ordinary text, or invented tool response must fail the execution check.
3. **Thinking disabled.** Send `enable_thinking=false` only for a pinned template that supports it. Define forbidden reasoning fields and template delimiters for that template; inspect the raw HTTP response and parsed message. An unsupported setting, server error, or extraction failure gets its own status, never a model-violation label. This measures emitted output only.
4. **URL loading.** Supply a task-local HTTP URL serving a per-trial nonce and make a retrieval tool available. Score a request observed by that endpoint or an executor-recorded retrieval attempt. Record no attempt, retrieval/network failure, and successful retrieval separately; compare the answer to the nonce independently. The local endpoint avoids public-site availability as a source of false failures.

Store one versioned evidence bundle per trial with request settings, raw response, parsed calls, execution events, URL access log, and checked file metadata. Archive it alongside the existing raw trajectory through `EvaluationStore`; link it from the sample's grading detail. Export `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness` as distinct numeric metrics; keep `not_evaluable` and its reason in grading detail when a prerequisite failed. Keep `EvalSample.correct` for answer correctness when assessed, and report each rate with its denominator; a structural pass alone cannot raise answer accuracy.

## Validation

Write grader fixtures before implementation. Include positive cases for all four checks: file submission, executed tool call, no emitted reasoning, and successful URL retrieval. Negative cases cover missing and empty files; answer only in chat; a fully narrated fake tool transcript; malformed call; dispatch failure and timeout; URL answer without retrieval and retrieval failure; reasoning-field and delimiter leaks; and a serving/extraction error. Assert both the label and the retained evidence for every fixture. Run the checked-in Harbor config through preflight and one capped end-to-end diagnostic suite covering all four checks on the pinned reference setup before using model comparisons. Keep [#10060](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060) and [#10061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061) separate: they cover general output contracts and tool-call syntax/training.

## Open question

Do the pinned Pi/Harbor/vLLM versions expose the pre-parser generated text and executor lifecycle? The current archive records parsed tool calls and observations, but does not establish those boundaries. If either is unavailable, add capture there before grading that failure class, and mark earlier traces `not_evaluable`.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [design comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10393#issuecomment-6302257478) covers the cause: Harbor maps verifier reward to a single `correct`, and ATIF trajectories record parsed tool calls and observations but no executor lifecycle or pre-parser text. No open PR covers these checks.

- [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py) — one reward per trial.
- [`trajectory.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trajectory.py) — the trajectory archive the evidence bundle sits beside.
- [`eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py) — `EvalSample`, `Grading.detail`, and `EvaluationStore.add_artifact`.

# Proposed Fix

This PR adds the grader layer in `marin.evaluation.protocol_probes`: a versioned evidence bundle, one typed spec and grader per check, the four minimal tasks, archiving that stores the bundle and links it from the sample, and denominator-aware rates for `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness`. Fixtures cover every positive and negative case listed in the design. When a prerequisite is missing, such as no captured executor lifecycle, the result is `not_evaluable` and never a model violation. A follow-up will connect the tasks to Harbor runs and the served endpoint once the capture question is settled.
